arxiv:2609.25845.title: Visual Jev: Accurate and Efficient Decisions from Shared Visual Context
arxiv:2609.25845.relationship: An independent vision–language decision model. It is not a TypeSafe product and is not evidence that hosted Jev accepts images.
arxiv:2609.25845.summary: Encodes an image and public context once, runs isolated question suffixes as a batch, and reads candidate probabilities from the backbone’s LM head. The design separates four effects: model quality, readout, prefix sharing and batching.
arxiv:2609.25845.task: Forced-choice visual questions on GQA, SNLI-VE, TextVQA and TallyQA with Qwen3-VL-4B (8B extension) on one RTX 5090.
baselines: untuned backbone read through its LM head
arxiv:2609.25845.finding: Post-training raised equal-weight macro accuracy from 0.706 to 0.761; with 32 questions per image, shared batched execution was 8.9× faster (warm, amortized) than independent serial calls and 3.4× faster than batching that recomputes the prefix.
caveats: 5.7 ms is amortized: a 32-question batch completes in about 182 ms. It is not the latency of an independent request.
Accuracy gains concentrate on the two task families represented in training.
A matched typed head showed no consistent accuracy advantage over the LM-head readout.
Single-machine study on a consumer GPU; queueing latency is excluded.

arxiv:2609.26532.title: REFLEX with Jev for Efficient Selective Control in LLM Agents
arxiv:2609.26532.relationship: Uses hosted jev-1.13.0 as a typed decision layer inside an LLM agent, calling a strong LLM when confidence is low or generation is required.
arxiv:2609.26532.summary: Compares strong-only, cheap-generative-cascade and Jev-gated agents on a frozen 100-task benchmark, adds controlled interventions on action-set size and near-valid alternatives, and checks external BFCL and τ-style tasks.
arxiv:2609.26532.task: Tool-using agent decisions on REFLEX-Sim (100 frozen tasks); BFCL function selection; 300 τ-style episodes over 60 paired tasks.
arxiv:2609.26532.finding: At threshold τ = 0.5, REFLEX reached 95% success with 1.12 strong-model calls per task, against 88% and 4.10 calls for the strong-only agent (72.7% fewer strong calls).
caveats: Only one proprietary decision model is tested.
On BFCL ordinary routing is near-saturated; on τ-style episodes a cheap generative cascade remains competitive.
The τ evaluation is a 300-episode held-out validation, not a full leaderboard; API costs are dated snapshots.
Action-set size and ambiguity effects concentrate in authority and risk families.

arxiv:2609.26550.title: JEV-as-a-Judge: Accept When Confident, Escalate When Unsure
arxiv:2609.26550.relationship: Evaluates hosted jev-1.13.0 as a model judge against sixteen generative and reward-model judges.
arxiv:2609.26550.summary: Uses Jev as a decision-only judge whose confidence decides whether to accept its verdict or escalate to a reasoning judge. Sixteen generative and reward-model judges are compared on identical items with blinded human adjudication of disagreements, thresholds are frozen before held-out evaluation, and a pre-specified live test covers two new workloads.
arxiv:2609.26550.task: Pairwise preference, evidence-grounded factuality and final-answer adjudication (5,172 base judgments), with follow-ups on four-way selection, answer style and natural prose, and a prospective test on two new correctness workloads.
datasets: PPE and JudgeBench Claude split (570 live pairs)
baselines: 13 hosted judges incl. GPT-6 Astra, Claude Sonnet 5, Gemini 3.1 Pro
arxiv:2609.26550.finding: Jev came within three points of GPT-6 wherever the verdict could be read off the text, at 0.36% of its fee and a 0.15 s median latency, and fell behind where the verdict had to be derived (math, code, logic). A cascade with a threshold frozen in advance beat GPT-6 by 0.9 points on 1,610 held-out pairs at 41% of its fee, and in a pre-specified live test on two new workloads it matched GPT-6’s accuracy exactly.
caveats: Comparators were added in rounds after initial results were known; only the frozen policies, the primary adjudication and the prospective test were fixed in advance.
Human adjudication covers 183 disagreement-selected items annotated by one team member.
Latency comes from one client location; apart from the live test, cascade fees and latencies are simulated offline.
Confidence routing weakens on style-adversarial pairs and reference-free prose.

arxiv:2609.26758.title: Type-Safe Is Not Error-Free: A Constrained Decision Head Follows the Option Name, Not the Rubric Bound to It
arxiv:2609.26758.relationship: Black-box evaluation of hosted Jev alongside two open-weight Jev-like encoder decision heads.
arxiv:2609.26758.summary: Holds question, state, rubric wording and the set of option names fixed and changes only which name is bound to which rubric. The study separates type validity (0% type errors by construction) from name invariance, ranking quality and test–retest noise across three read-out families.
arxiv:2609.26758.task: Binary workflow decisions with task-specific rubrics (1,200 items over 4 predicates), plus generic-rubric, multi-way (683 questions) and random-name arms.
arxiv:2609.26758.finding: Rebinding the rubrics behind no/yes lowered hosted Jev’s AUROC from .8146 to .5806 and flipped 32.50% of its answers (neutral names: ~2%; 24× its test–retest floor) while type errors stayed at 0%. The steeper .94→.23 inversion comes from an open marker head, not from Jev.
caveats: The .9376→.2315 AUROC inversion belongs to an open marker-readout checkpoint, not to hosted Jev.
One released checkpoint per open read-out geometry; English only.
The hosted model is a non-deterministic black box observed at one point in time; no model version is pinned.
The multi-way arm rests on a pool with shipped accuracy .5637 and is directional.
Mitigations (neutral identifiers; randomising names in training) are proposed, not evaluated.

arxiv:2609.24574.title: Evaluating Decision Models for Text Annotation in Computational Social Science
arxiv:2609.24574.relationship: Evaluates hosted Jev and open-weight decision models against 19 LLMs under one zero-shot protocol.
arxiv:2609.24574.summary: Replicates an 18-task computational-social-science suite to ask whether decision models can serve as annotators. Accuracy, measured cost and calibration are reported together, and low-confidence routing to an LLM is tested.
arxiv:2609.24574.task: 18 CSS classification tasks (7,977 items: 3 for selection, 15 for evaluation); an appendix extends to open decision models.
arxiv:2609.24574.finding: Jev trailed the per-task best LLM on 14 of 15 tasks (median −11.6 macro-F1) at a median 44× lower measured cost. Routing low-confidence items to an LLM matched or exceeded the LLM alone at a quarter to half of its cost.

Verbalised LLM confidence and native probabilities are different signals; baselines that decline to estimate are excluded from calibration.
Older public corpora may overlap with training data; the overlap is unknown.

arxiv:2609.28587.title: NumericJev: Jev-like LLM Numerical Decoding with Multiway Decision Trees

Bit, digit and threshold numerical encodings

Arithmetic benchmark built by the authors.

arxiv:2609.28613.title: Decision Hijacking: Prompt Injection Attacks on Jev's Typed Probabilistic Decisions
arxiv:2609.28613.relationship: Black-box prompt-injection study of hosted jev-1.13.0 on reconstructed agent tool-use cases.

caveats: One proprietary version; three-choice primary space.
Measures selection, not harmful execution.
Success concentrates in cases with small initial decision margins.

claims.headline: Injection shifts probabilities (+0.043) but rarely selects the target (1.8%)

limitations: Three-way action space; larger action sets not established.
Selection, not executed harm.

claims.headline: Score feedback doubles attacker probability; success 1.8% → 3.5%

limitations: Exploratory link to decision margins.
Requires access to returned probabilities.

arxiv:2609.28919.title: Harness Tokenomics: A Router for the Enterprise Agentic Control Plane

One vendor’s list prices.
Routing quality is assumed from cache and payback rules, not validated against outcomes.

User pauses move the saving as much as the classifier does.

Single author.

arxiv:2609.29283.title: From Text Decisions to Pixels: An Study of Jev-Style Visual Choice Model
arxiv:2609.29283.relationship: Builds an independent Jev-style visual choice interface on small open multimodal models; hosted Jev is not evaluated.

Specialist probes still lead on recognition.
No released code located.

arxiv:2609.29429.title: Just Ask Jev: Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions as a Zero-Shot Detector of AI Alignment Failures
arxiv:2609.29429.relationship: Benchmarks hosted jev-1.13.0 as a zero-shot detector of alignment failures in other models’ outputs.
arxiv:2609.29429.summary: Builds RLCDAlignBench from 44 benchmarks covering ten alignment failures (sycophancy, jailbreaks, deception, injection, hallucination, privacy, bias, reward hacking, concealed uncertainty, power seeking) on five target models, varying what Jev is asked and what it sees.
arxiv:2609.29429.task: Zero-shot detection of alignment failures in model transcripts.
datasets: Outputs of Qwen3.5-2B, Phi-4-mini, Gemma-2-2B, Llama-3.2-3B, Olmo-3-7B
arxiv:2609.29429.finding: A generic yes/no question ranked most failures well (median AUROC 0.886 over 31 benchmarks) at about 1/63 of the judges’ cost, but probabilities did not transfer as thresholds (median ECE 0.168 against a null of 0.074); supplying the reference that defines a failure gave the large gains.
caveats: Many failures are relational: the detector must be given the defining reference.
Labels are mostly benchmark-judge labels; two benchmarks have human labels.
Small target models.

code.note: Benchmark, cached Jev answers and rescoring scripts.

claims.headline: Zero-shot failure detection: median AUROC 0.886 at 1/63 of judge cost

limitations: Supplying the defining reference matters more than added context (e.g. PrivacyLens 0.79 → 0.95).

limitations: Base rates differ by benchmark.

arxiv:2609.29769.title: JEV vs. LLMs as Rubric Judges: Cheaper, Faster, and Wrong in the Same Places
arxiv:2609.29769.relationship: Compares hosted Jev 1.13 with three flash-tier LLM judges on rubric judging against human labels.
arxiv:2609.29769.summary: Gives Jev and GPT-5.6 Luna, Gemini 3.8 Flash and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash identical criterion texts on 5,003 pairs from nine panels of seven benchmarks with human judgments, both per criterion and as whole rubrics, and replays cascades.

caveats: Observational: expectations formed on binary panels and tested on ordinal ones.
Ordinal labels follow unstated rating conventions that all judges miss.
Flash-tier judges only.

claims.headline: Parity on most rubric criteria at 1/16–1/325 of the cost
claims.text: Against per-criterion LLM judges, Jev differed significantly in only 8 of 27 paired accuracy comparisons and reached parity in 8 more; the LLM judges cost 16 to 325 times as much and took 28 to 350 times as long.
limitations: Behind on ordinal criteria; flash-tier comparators.

claims.headline: Judges share Jev’s confident errors (96%); cascades gain ≤2.7 points
claims.text: On Jev’s most confident errors, 96.0% of LLM verdicts repeated its answer against 50.3% expected under independence, and cascades beat the best single judge by at most 2.7 points even with oracle thresholds.

arxiv:2609.30186.title: Jev-Mobile: Jev as an Executor for Mobile GUI Agents
arxiv:2609.30186.relationship: Uses hosted Jev as the action executor of a mobile GUI agent planned by a vision–language model.

The executor was not ablated against other choice models.

arxiv:2609.30216.title: Jev in the Wild: A Data-Driven Analysis of the Jev Model's Functionality, Applications and Ecosystem

Labels assigned by an LLM agent with a second LLM review.
Stars measure attention, not use or quality.

arxiv:2609.30243.title: JevOut: Natural Context Can Flip Decision Models
arxiv:2609.30243.relationship: Searches for natural context additions that flip hosted jev-1.13.0 and open Jev-like systems from correct to chosen wrong answers.
arxiv:2609.30243.summary: Fixes a wrong target option for each initially correct item and uses returned option probabilities to refine short, fluent context additions that leave the source, question, options and gold answer unchanged.
arxiv:2609.30243.task: Targeted redirection of decisions by natural context across reasoning, routing and policy tasks.
datasets: 700 held-out items from seven decision datasets
arxiv:2609.30243.finding: Within 64 accepted target evaluations, optimised context redirected 312 of 508 initially correct Jev decisions (61.4%), with 229 reaching at least 0.7 probability on the wrong target; a single target-aware addition flipped 16.9% against 2.2% for a neutral addition.
caveats: Additions are optimised with probability feedback.
Fluency judged by a model, not by people.
One hosted version.

claims.headline: Natural context flips 61% of correct decisions (vs 2% neutral)
claims.text: Within 64 accepted target evaluations, optimised natural context redirected 312 of 508 initially correct decisions (61.4%, Wilson 57.1–65.5%), 229 of them with at least 0.7 probability on the wrong target; one target-aware addition flipped 16.9% against 2.2% for a neutral one.

arxiv:2609.30454.title: Auditing System-1 Models on Biosecurity-Relevant Benchmarks: Calibration, Selective Prediction, and Permutation Instability in a Non-Generative Model
arxiv:2609.30454.relationship: Audits hosted jev-1.13.0 on biosecurity-relevant multiple-choice benchmarks for calibration, selective prediction and option-order stability.
arxiv:2609.30454.summary: Scores 6,020 items from WMDP, a paraphrase-robust WMDP-Bio variant and six LAB-Bench subtasks, establishes how the vendor’s confidence field relates to the returned probabilities, and separates option-order effects from run-to-run variation.
arxiv:2609.30454.finding: Read correctly, the confidence field is calibrated overall (pooled ECE 0.034, AUROC 0.820) and deferring the least confident 40% raised WMDP-Bio accuracy from 85.2% to 97.1%; but four cyclic option rotations changed the answer on 37.4% of WMDP-Cyber items, 28.2 points beyond run-to-run variation.
caveats: WMDP accuracy is a proxy for hazardous knowledge, not a capability claim.
Per-task calibration varies widely (ECE 0.033–0.193).
One hosted version.

claims.headline: Confidence = chance-normalised max probability; pooled ECE 0.034
claims.text: The vendor’s confidence field matched a chance-normalised maximum probability for 97.9% of 6,020 records; read that way, pooled ECE was 0.034 and AUROC 0.820 for separating correct from incorrect answers, with per-task ECE from 0.033 to 0.193.
limitations: Pooling flatters calibration; per-task values matter.

claims.headline: Option rotation changes 37% of answers; aggregate accuracy hides it
claims.text: Under four cyclic rotations of the answer options, 37.4% of WMDP-Cyber items received different answers against 9.2% across four identical calls, leaving 28.2 points attributable to option order (WMDP-Bio: 10.6% vs 2.4%); aggregate accuracy moved by under 1.3 points.
limitations: Multiple-choice items with 2–10 options.

arxiv:2609.30706.title: LAVOIR: Teaching a Single-Pass Decision Encoder When and What to Ask with Amortized Value of Information
arxiv:2609.30706.relationship: Extends the open Laya encoder with a value-of-information head so a single-pass decision model can ask before deciding.
arxiv:2609.30706.summary: Places candidate pieces of missing information next to the answer options so one forward pass returns both the decision distribution and, for each slot, the expected gain from asking about it; trained on schema-generated dialogues and tested on real customer-service data.

arxiv:2609.30706.finding: With group temperatures, the learned policy reached an accuracy–questions AUC of 0.799–0.800 against 0.800–0.803 for the oracle, with 88–92% top-1 agreement on which slot to ask about; zero-shot decisions stayed 15 points below the Bayes ceiling.
caveats: Synthetic dialogues from a simulator; real-data tests cover single exchanges.
Laya and Jev comparison figures are taken from other reports.

claims.headline: Learned “when to ask” policy ≈ oracle (AUC 0.80 vs 0.80)
claims.text: A value-of-information head trained alongside the decision head matched an oracle asking policy closely (accuracy–questions AUC 0.799–0.800 vs 0.800–0.803) and chose the same slot to ask about in 88–92% of cases.
limitations: Synthetic dialogues; the head does not learn that value vanishes as certainty grows out of distribution.

arxiv:2609.30922.title: JevSoup: System-One Routing for Training-Free LoRA Composition
arxiv:2609.30922.relationship: Uses hosted jev-1.13.0 to pick LoRA experts for training-free adapter composition.

claims.text: Choosing two LoRA experts with Jev and composing them orthogonally beat the strongest external baseline by 1.13, 1.19 and 0.21 macro points at 1.7B, 4B and 8B.

arxiv:2609.31142.title: JevAdvBench: A Benchmark and Black-Box Attacks for Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions Models
arxiv:2609.31142.relationship: Adversarial benchmark and black-box attacks for hosted jev-1.13.0, scored against the model’s own clean decisions and a re-run noise floor.

arxiv:2609.33209.title: Beyond Calibration: Do a Typed-Decision Model's Probabilities Obey the Probability Axioms?

arxiv:2609.33401.title: Evaluating System One Models for Agent Security Decisions: Reliability, Calibration, and Selective Automation
arxiv:2609.33401.relationship: Evaluates hosted Jev 1.13 and three open Jev-like models (Laya, Decider, Nimble) as security checks for tool-using agents.
arxiv:2609.33401.summary: Compares decision models with specialised classifiers and LLM judges on prompt-injection detection, interaction-risk judgment and harmful-request screening, then asks how many inputs a fixed policy can process automatically within error limits.

caveats: Benchmarks differ in label construction; group-level failures need group-level tests.
Thresholds chosen on development data did not always transfer.

code.note: Experiment code, final predictions, partitions and analyses.

claims.text: Under a fixed symmetric review policy, Jev could automate only 7.63% of R-Judge inputs within the miss and blocking limits; choosing block and allow thresholds separately raised coverage to 47.03%, entirely through additional blocks.
limitations: Coverage depends on error limits set by the authors.

claims.headline: Open Jev-like models: Laya AUROC 0.53 vs Jev 0.96 on R-Judge
claims.text: On shared R-Judge inputs, Laya’s AUROC was 0.533 against Jev’s 0.961 and its Brier score 0.272 against 0.103 — worse than a constant base-rate forecast; Bespoke Nimble led WAInjectBench yet flagged 92.8% of benign R-Judge interactions as unsafe.
limitations: Open checkpoints run as shipped, without task adaptation.

arxiv:2609.33538.title: Jev Matches 7B Language Models for Speech-Neuroprosthesis Rescoring
arxiv:2609.33538.relationship: Uses hosted Jev to rescore candidate sentences of a speech neuroprosthesis decoder, against 7B language models.
arxiv:2609.33538.summary: Poses the final rescoring stage of a brain-to-text decoder as one typed decision with a probability per candidate sentence, combined with the decoder’s own score, and compares Jev, Laya, OPT-6.7b and Qwen2.5-7B on held-out sentences from a participant with ALS.
arxiv:2609.33538.task: Rescoring n-best sentence candidates from neural speech decoding.
arxiv:2609.33538.finding: Jev reached 7.5% word error against 7.8% for both 7B models (6.9% vs 7.2% and 7.4% with the decoder weight re-tuned), at $0.07 per thousand sentences and without a GPU; general LLMs asked to pick a sentence answered from list position.
caveats: One participant and one decoder.
Closed model: the result shows that a typed decision model can do the job, not why.
Internet latency (262 ms end to end) is not faster than a local 7B model (27 ms).

claims.headline: Rescoring: WER 7.5% vs 7.8% for 7B LLMs, no GPU needed
claims.text: On 978 held-out sentences, Jev rescoring reached 7.46% word error against 7.80% for OPT-6.7b and 7.75% for Qwen2.5-7B (decoder alone 8.1%), at $0.07 per thousand sentences; end-to-end latency was 262 ms over the internet against 27 ms for a local 7B model.
limitations: One participant; one decoder.

arxiv:2609.33671.title: COGNIT-Guard: Calibrated Standalone Direct-Decision Guardrails with Heterogeneous CPU-NPU Confidence Cascading under Explicit Latency and False-Positive Constraints
arxiv:2609.33671.relationship: Builds a safety guardrail around the open Laya-322M direct-decision model with a confidence-gated CPU–NPU cascade.
arxiv:2609.33671.summary: Adapts Laya-322M on dual-use boundary pairs, places a calibrated CPU gatekeeper in front of it, and escalates uncertain prompts to the NPU-resident model under latency and false-positive constraints.
arxiv:2609.33671.task: Pre-ingestion safety screening of prompts with dual-use false-positive control.
arxiv:2609.33671.finding: After supervised boundary adaptation the cascade reached 98.85% accuracy, 0.42% benign false-positive rate and 1.12% ECE on DUCS-Bench (zero-shot Laya ROC-AUC 0.827 vs 0.997 adapted), but in-domain adaptation cost out-of-distribution accuracy (60.33% → 56.81%), partly recovered with replay.
caveats: Single author; one in-house benchmark for the main result.
Zero-shot Laya is far weaker than the adapted model.

code.note: Code, evaluation scripts and DUCS-Bench release.
code.label: Available

claims.headline: Adapted open guard: AUC 0.83 → 0.997, with an OOD “alignment tax”
claims.text: Boundary adaptation raised Laya-322M from ROC-AUC 0.827 zero-shot to 0.997 on DUCS-Bench with 0.42% benign false positives, while out-of-distribution accuracy on SafetyBench-ZH fell from 60.33% to 56.81% before replay recovered it to 64–65%.
limitations: In-house benchmark; NPU-specific latency.

arxiv:2609.33689.title: Type-Safe Decision Frameworks for Agentic 5G Control: A Theory-Driven Testbed Characterization of Where They Can Be Applied
arxiv:2609.33689.relationship: Characterises hosted jev-1.13.0, the open Laya encoder and the AnyJev LLM readout as typed decision layers in a 5G core-policy testbed.
arxiv:2609.33689.summary: Turns timeliness, type conformance, certification cost and cardinality into checkable applicability predicates and measures each on an Open5GS/UERANSIM testbed with a closed policy loop.
arxiv:2609.33689.task: Network control decisions (handover, anomaly severity, SLA breach, slice admission) under deadlines.
arxiv:2609.33689.finding: Jev read new, runtime-declared questions without labels (≥0.98 on six of eight counterfactual templates) but reached only 0.67 on rule-defined known classes against 0.90–0.92 for fine-tuned specialists, and its network-bound latency (warm p50 281 ms, cold 726 ms) never met the 100 ms near-real-time classes.
caveats: Single testbed; real-time factor scaling of RAN timing.
Data leave the operator’s domain with a hosted model.

claims.headline: Hosted Jev never meets 100 ms near-RT deadlines (warm p50 281 ms)
claims.text: Jev’s median latency from the testbed was network-bound (TCP connection alone 199 ms; warm p50 281 ms, cold 726 ms) and never reached the 100 ms class, while local specialists stayed within about 30 ms at p99; a co-located decoding LLM made 12–56% of local decisions miss 100 ms.
limitations: One site and network path.

claims.headline: Zero-shot Jev 0.67 on rule-defined classes vs 0.90–0.92 for specialists
claims.text: On rule-defined known decision classes, zero-shot Jev reached 0.67 accuracy against 0.92 for a fine-tuned encoder and 0.90 for fine-tuned Laya, yet it answered at least 0.98 on six of eight new counterfactual question templates and gained when the rule was stated (anomaly severity 0.347 → 0.880).
limitations: Specialists answer only the questions they were trained on.

arxiv:2609.33843.title: Laya as a Typed Probabilistic Assessor: An Independent Reproduction and a Preregistered Study of Calibration and Selective Escalation
arxiv:2609.33843.relationship: Independent, preregistered reproduction of the open Laya Typed-Decisions checkpoint’s accuracy, calibration and selective escalation.
arxiv:2609.33843.summary: Re-runs the released 421M ModernBERT-large checkpoint on its official benchmark, tests preregistered calibration and escalation hypotheses with false-discovery control, and probes out-of-distribution transfer.
arxiv:2609.33843.task: Typed choice, yes/no and score questions over workflow state.
arxiv:2609.33843.finding: The reproduction matched the card’s accuracy (0.767 vs 0.766) but found the checkpoint uniformly under-confident (signed gap −0.214, every reliability bin below its accuracy), the opposite of the card’s warning; one temperature (T = 0.469) cut held-out ECE from 0.204 to 0.037, and the escalation gate missed its 10% error target.
caveats: Single checkpoint; benchmark labels come from a synthetic 4B-class teacher whose self-agreement (0.735) the model exceeds.
No zero-shot transfer out of distribution (accuracy 0.617).

code.note: Run manifests and preregistration in ancillary files.
code.label: Partial

claims.headline: Open Laya checkpoint under-confident (gap −0.214); one temperature fixes it
claims.text: The shipped Laya checkpoint reproduced its card accuracy (0.767 vs 0.766) but was uniformly under-confident — signed confidence–accuracy gap −0.214 with every occupied bin’s accuracy above its confidence — and a single temperature of 0.469 cut held-out ECE from 0.204 to 0.037.
limitations: Gold labels are a synthetic teacher’s answers.

arxiv:2609.33874.title: JET: Justification Evaluation in Transformer
arxiv:2609.33874.relationship: Builds a local, training-free candidate-likelihood decision method on open models and uses hosted Jev 1.13 as an external reference.
arxiv:2609.33874.summary: Scores a finite set of answers by their likelihood under pretrained language and vision–language models, sharing computation across candidates, and measures accuracy and throughput on consumer hardware.
arxiv:2609.33874.task: Multiple-choice decisions (full MMLU) and game-screen choices on local hardware.
arxiv:2609.33874.finding: The best local configuration reached 85.09% on full MMLU at 2.21 requests/s, 3.97 points below the author’s evaluation of Jev 1.13 (89.06% at 2.86 requests/s); prefix reuse and cache management gave 2.18–2.23× speedups with unchanged outputs.
caveats: Jev figure from a separate manual evaluation, not the same harness.
LoRA gain cannot be fully attributed (reference model from a separate conversion).
Single author.

claims.headline: Local likelihood readout 85.1% vs Jev 89.1% on MMLU
claims.text: On the 14,042-question MMLU test set, the best local candidate-likelihood configuration reached 85.09% at 2.21 requests/s, 3.97 points below the author’s evaluation of Jev 1.13 (89.06% at 2.86 requests/s).
limitations: Jev number from a separate manual run.

arxiv:2609.33971.title: Do System One Decisions Add Up? A Study of Probabilistic Coherence
arxiv:2609.33971.relationship: Tests whether hosted jev-1.13.0 and the open Laya checkpoint give coherent probabilities when one decision is broken into stages.
arxiv:2609.33971.summary: Compares direct fine-label predictions with broad-category probabilities and with predictions reconstructed through those categories on 2,500 matched examples per system.
arxiv:2609.33971.finding: Both systems disagreed with themselves across granularities (mean category-level total variation 0.219–0.349 for Jev, 0.424–0.689 for Laya); reconstructing through categories cut Jev’s CLINC150 accuracy by 22.9 points but raised Laya’s by 21.3.
caveats: Exploratory; scope narrowed after pilots.
Instructions, choices, ordering and calibration change together.
Three English closed-set datasets.

claims.headline: Staged decisions disagree with direct ones; Jev loses 22.9 points on CLINC150
claims.text: Across 72,000 classification questions, mean category-level total variation between direct and staged predictions was 0.219–0.349 for Jev and 0.424–0.689 for Laya; staging cut Jev’s CLINC150 accuracy by 22.9 points [−24.9, −20.9] and raised Laya’s by 21.3.
limitations: Hierarchies fixed by the authors.

arxiv:2609.34024.title: Jev in Medicine: A Benchmark Evaluation
arxiv:2609.34024.relationship: Benchmarks hosted Jev 1.13 on medical question answering and diagnostic reasoning against GPT-6 Sol.
arxiv:2609.34024.summary: Asks one Choice question per item on four medical benchmarks, comparing accuracy, calibration, selective prediction and recognition of unanswerable questions with GPT-6 Sol with and without reasoning.
baselines: GPT-6 Sol (medium reasoning and no reasoning)
arxiv:2609.34024.finding: Jev matched GPT-6 Sol on PubMedQA (78.4% vs 78.2%) but trailed on MetaMedQA (74.8% vs 82.7%) and far behind on DiagnosisArena-MCQ (59.8% vs 82.4%) and NEJM cases (61.8% vs 82.4%); it chose “I don’t know” on only 10.5% of 162 unanswerable questions. All 2,823 items cost US$0.08.
caveats: Text-only: images replaced by captions.
Reference answers used as published.
One version; no clinical validation.

claims.headline: Medicine: parity on abstracts, −22 points on diagnostic cases
claims.text: Jev’s accuracy matched GPT-6 Sol with medium reasoning on PubMedQA (78.4% vs 78.2%) but was lower on MetaMedQA (74.8% vs 82.7%) and much lower on DiagnosisArena-MCQ (59.8% vs 82.4%) and the NEJM Case Challenges (61.8% vs 82.4%).
limitations: Text-only inputs; examination-style items.

claims.headline: Picks “I don’t know” on 10.5% of unanswerable questions
claims.text: Of 162 questions whose correct answer was “I don’t know or cannot answer”, Jev chose that option for 10.5% (GPT-6 Sol 8.6%); on MetaMedQA its probabilities were better calibrated than GPT-6 Sol’s (ECE 0.063 vs 0.146).
limitations: Unanswerable items come from one benchmark.

arxiv:2609.34180.title: Decision Readouts for Text-Mediated Video Anomaly Detection: An Exploratory Evaluation of Jev and Qwen
arxiv:2609.34180.relationship: Exploratory comparison of hosted jev-1.13.0 decisions and Qwen readouts for text-mediated video anomaly detection.
arxiv:2609.34180.summary: Holds video-derived text evidence (summaries and ordered captions) fixed and compares Jev Noul and Choice decisions with three Qwen readouts on sampled anchors from two anomaly datasets.
arxiv:2609.34180.task: Video anomaly scoring from text descriptions.
arxiv:2609.34180.finding: On XD captions, Jev Noul reached 75.99% average precision against 48.47% for Qwen generated probability and 57.81% for the ordinal-likelihood readout (+18.18 points, 95% interval 5.53–31.50); UCF showed no corresponding advantage, and Jev Choice returned only 776 of 800 valid numerical answers.
caveats: Sparse development sample with few positives (10 and 37).
Text-mediated: depends on captioning quality.
Dataset-conditional result.

claims.headline: Same evidence, different readout: +18 AP on one dataset, none on the other
claims.text: With the same caption evidence, Jev Noul reached 75.99% AP on XD-Violence against 57.81% for the stronger Qwen ordinal-likelihood readout (+18.18 points, 95% interval 5.53–31.50); on UCF-Crime the ordinal readout instead had higher AUC (65.95% vs 52.26%).
limitations: Few positives; exploratory.

arxiv:2609.34227.title: When Does Selection Replace Extraction? A Pre-Registered Test of Agent Memory with a Typed Decision Model
arxiv:2609.34227.relationship: Pre-registered test of whether one hosted jev-1.13.0 selection call over raw conversation turns can replace LLM fact extraction in agent memory.
arxiv:2609.34227.summary: Compares raw turns selected by a single Jev call with an extraction-based memory at matched answer budgets on held-out conversations, with blind human grading.
arxiv:2609.34227.task: Long-term conversational memory for question answering.
arxiv:2609.34227.finding: At a tight budget, raw turns selected by Jev were non-inferior to an LLM-extraction memory (one-sided 95% bound −3.0 against a −5-point margin) and cost 3,061 times less to write; the reranking gain shrank from +17.4 to +1.5 points as the budget grew.
caveats: One benchmark family per setting; LoCoMo dialogues are LLM-generated.
Extraction baseline not run on LongMemEval.

claims.headline: One Jev selection call ≈ LLM-extraction memory at 1/3,061 the write cost
claims.text: At a tight budget on LoCoMo, raw turns selected by a single Jev call were non-inferior to an LLM-extraction memory (one-sided 95% bound −3.0 points against a −5-point margin) at 3,061 times lower write cost, and non-inferior to a gpt-4o-mini listwise reranker at about a third of its latency.
limitations: Human grading narrows the margin.
Gain depends on the answer budget.

arxiv:2609.34736.title: SeLMRoute: Probabilistic Semantic Evidence for Large Language Model Routing
arxiv:2609.34736.relationship: Uses typed decisions from hosted JEV (and, for comparison, Laya) as interpretable features for LLM routing.
arxiv:2609.34736.summary: Asks a decision model a fixed set of interpretable questions about each query, keeps the answers as probability distributions, and trains a light router on this semantic state to predict candidate-model performance.
arxiv:2609.34736.task: Routing queries among candidate LLMs (quality and quality–cost).
arxiv:2609.34736.finding: SeLMRoute reached 72.08% average accuracy against 69.23% for the strongest single model; the 40-dimensional probability state beat 88 hard features, dense embeddings and TF-IDF, and the JEV-based state outperformed the Laya-based one.
caveats: Single benchmark framework; published routers use a different split.
Requires a decision-model call per query.

claims.headline: Typed-question features route LLMs: 72.1% vs 69.2% best single model
claims.text: Routing on JEV’s probability answers to interpretable questions reached 72.08% average accuracy on LLMRouterBench against 69.23% for the strongest single model, and a JEV-based semantic state outperformed a Laya-based one.
limitations: One benchmark; split differs from published routers.

arxiv:2609.34862.title: JEV as a Judge for Agent Trace Security: An Empirical Comparison with Generative LLM Judges
arxiv:2609.34862.relationship: Compares hosted JEV with four generative LLM judges for retrospective security classification of agent trajectories.
arxiv:2609.34862.summary: Applies a common risk rubric with behaviour-level labels to 5,219 trajectories from four benchmark collections and compares positive-class F1, coverage, latency and cost.
arxiv:2609.34862.task: Retrospective safety judgment of tool-using agent traces.
baselines: GLM-5.2 and three other generative judges
arxiv:2609.34862.finding: JEV reached a benchmark-averaged positive-class F1 of 77.8 against 74.1 for the strongest generative judge (GLM-5.2), leading on ATBench500 and MCPHunt but trailing on R-Judge and TraceSafe, at 0.99 s median latency and about $0.000195 per judgment.
caveats: Common threshold; performance varies by dataset.
Valid-result coverage 95.5%.
No version or code stated.

claims.headline: Trace security: F1 77.8 vs 74.1 for the best LLM judge
claims.text: Across four trace-security benchmarks (5,219 trajectories), JEV’s benchmark-averaged positive-class F1 was 77.8 against 74.1 for GLM-5.2, with a 2.7-point paired advantage [0.5, 4.8]; median latency 0.99 s and about $0.000195 per valid judgment.
limitations: Leads on two of four datasets; GLM more precise overall.

arxiv:2609.34963.title: JevVibe: Efficient Classification-Guided Secure Code Generation
arxiv:2609.34963.relationship: Uses hosted jev-1.13.0 to classify security weaknesses in generated code and to guide repair.
arxiv:2609.34963.summary: Compares Jev with six open-weight autoregressive models and GPT-5.6-Sol on 50-way CWE classification, then feeds the predicted weakness to a repair model.
arxiv:2609.34963.task: CWE classification and classification-guided secure code repair.
arxiv:2609.34963.finding: Jev beat all six open models (Top-1 0.458 vs 0.335 for Qwen2.5-Coder-32B) but trailed GPT-5.6-Sol on Top-1 (0.495) while leading on Top-3/Top-5, at $0.283 against $15.83 and 0.244 s against 1.531 s median latency; Jev-guided repair raised the security pass rate from 63.5% to 70.7% (LLM-guided 66.1%).
caveats: One benchmark; detector-based pass rate.
Top-1 below the frontier model.

claims.headline: CWE triage: Top-1 0.46 vs 0.50 (frontier) at 1/56 of the cost
claims.text: On 50-way CWE classification, Jev reached Top-1 0.458 (GPT-5.6-Sol 0.495; best open model 0.335) and Top-5 0.836, at $0.283 against $15.83 and a 0.244 s against 1.531 s median latency; Jev-guided repair raised the security pass rate to 70.7% against 66.1% for LLM-guided repair.
limitations: Pass rate measured by the benchmark’s own detector.

arxiv:2609.34969.title: NavJev: Efficient Vision-Language Navigation via Action-Centric Visual Compression and Discriminative Action-Semantic Memory
arxiv:2609.34969.relationship: Uses hosted Jev for typed action selection in zero-shot vision-and-language navigation after compressing views into text.
arxiv:2609.34969.summary: Turns candidate waypoint views into compact textual action descriptions (geometry, captions, semantic tags), filters shared semantics, and asks Jev to choose the next action.
baselines: Qwen3.8-Max and GPT-4o as decision layers
arxiv:2609.34969.finding: NavJev reached 27.0% success and 22.4% SPL at 0.65 s per step, 41.5× faster than Open-Nav (which reached 19.0% SR with GPT-4o); used as the decision layer, Jev beat Qwen3.8-Max and GPT-4o by 2.0 and 13.0 SR points at 0.53 s per decision.
caveats: Low absolute success; compression components carry much of the gain (SR 19 → 27 in the ablation).
Text-only decisions depend on captioners.

claims.headline: Navigation: 27% SR at 0.65 s/step; components, not just Jev, carry the gain
claims.text: On R2R-CE, NavJev reached 27.0% SR and 22.4% SPL at 0.65 s per step (Open-Nav with GPT-4o: 19.0% SR at 27.0 s); in the ablation, the compression and memory components raised SR from 19.0% to 27.0% with Jev fixed.
limitations: 100-episode ablation split.

arxiv:2609.35286.title: The Argument and the Letterhead: Source-Position Coherence in AI Evaluation
arxiv:2609.35286.relationship: Preregistered study of whether AI evaluators separate an argument’s quality from its stated source, with a later supplement on hosted Jev 1.13.0.
arxiv:2609.35286.summary: Rates six fixed policy texts under several source attributions with chat models and, in a separately registered supplement, with Jev’s native scoring rubric.
arxiv:2609.35286.task: Argument-strength rating under varied source attribution.
datasets: Six policy texts (US AI policy, German debt brake, Swiss nuclear energy)
baselines: GPT-5.6 Sol and other chat models
arxiv:2609.35286.finding: Source–argument interactions appeared across chat models; the Jev supplement (288 ratings) also showed five interactions above the adopted 0.05 reference, though its distinct rubric and interrupted collection limit comparison.
caveats: Descriptive studies; the Jev supplement uses a different rubric.
Small number of fixed texts.

claims.headline: Jev’s argument scores move with the stated source
claims.text: In a separately registered supplement of 288 ratings, Jev’s scores of the same German and Swiss policy arguments varied with the stated source, with five source–argument interactions above the 0.05 reference adopted for the chat models.
limitations: Different rubric from the chat models; interrupted collection.

arxiv:2609.35293.title: Decide, Don't Generate: Competitive Dimensional ABSA with Jev's Typed Decisions
arxiv:2609.35293.relationship: Builds a SemEval-2026 dimensional aspect-based sentiment system from hosted jev-1.13.0 decisions without generation or backbone tuning.
arxiv:2609.35293.summary: Decomposes valence–arousal regression, triplet and quadruplet extraction into Choice, Score and Noul questions and aligns them with the annotation scheme through 488 coefficients fitted on CPU.
arxiv:2609.35293.task: Dimensional aspect-based sentiment analysis in six languages.
datasets: SemEval-2026 Task III Track A (ten corpora, six languages)
arxiv:2609.35293.finding: The system reached 1.0645 RMSE on valence–arousal regression, the lowest aggregate error of any participating system, and 52.09 / 44.06 continuous F1 on triplet and quadruplet extraction, above fine-tuned 70B and 120B baselines; supervised calibration roughly halved the raw regression error.
caveats: Uses labelled data for 488 fitted coefficients.
Extraction errors remain structural (span proposal and selection).

claims.headline: SemEval ABSA: best regression error with 488 fitted coefficients
claims.text: Without generating text or tuning a backbone, the Jev-based system reached 1.0645 RMSE on ten-corpus valence–arousal regression, the lowest aggregate of any SemEval-2026 participant, and supervised calibration of its scores roughly halved the raw error.
limitations: Calibration fits benchmark labels.

arxiv:2609.35342.title: Jev thinks "I don't know'', but doesn't say it: Introducing Sys1Cal-v1 Dataset for Probability Calibration
arxiv:2609.35342.relationship: Introduces a dataset with known ground-truth probabilities and uses it to test whether hosted Jev’s option probabilities have the right numerical meaning.
arxiv:2609.35342.summary: Builds 365 rendered True/False items from 92 problems whose exact probability is known (explicit, frequency, compound, conditional, Bayes, sequential updates) and queries each through Noul, Choice and Score, measuring distance from the true distribution.
arxiv:2609.35342.finding: Noul and Score answers were close to the true probabilities (soft accuracy 0.918 and 0.886) but Choice answers were not (0.764; SemIf 0.629); estimating an implicit “unknown” component lifted Choice to 0.931.
caveats: Synthetic; isolates probability semantics rather than broad competence.
Single author; Score needs a projection to True/False.

claims.headline: Known-probability test: Noul 0.92, Score 0.89, Choice 0.76
claims.text: Against exactly known probabilities, Jev’s Noul and Score answers reached soft accuracy 0.918 and 0.886 but its Choice answers only 0.764 (SemIf 0.629); modelling an implicit “unknown” share raised Choice to 0.931.
limitations: Synthetic propositions.

arxiv:2609.35865.title: PACT: Pairwise-Anchored Calibrated Tuning for Single-Token Typed Decisions
arxiv:2609.35865.relationship: Proposes a contrastive, calibration-aware training objective for open single-token typed decision models, starting from the open Nimble recipe.
arxiv:2609.35865.summary: Turns certificate-verified contrastive pairs into four extra training terms (a pair margin, permutation consistency, evidence necessity and ordinal transport) and reproduces the released Nimble recipe in the same harness with pre-stated falsification tests.
arxiv:2609.35865.task: Single-token typed decisions over workflow contexts (choice, yes/no, rubric scores).
arxiv:2609.35865.finding: PACT did not beat the properly reproduced Nimble recipe on accuracy (84.6% vs 85.2%) or calibration, but it had the lowest position bias (answer flips under relabelling 9.8% vs 13.8%) and ordinal error, and against a cross-entropy control it halved seed-to-seed spread and cut NLL by 26%.
caveats: No single term raises raw accuracy; gains are in robustness and stability.
One curated dataset and backbone.

code.note: Code, splits, adapters and run records.
code.label: Available

claims.headline: Open recipe holds up; extra terms buy robustness, not accuracy
claims.text: Properly reproduced, the released Nimble recipe stayed the most accurate and best-calibrated run (85.2%, ECE 5.4%); PACT reached 84.6% but cut answer flips under relabelling from 13.8% to 9.8% and Score MAE from 0.311 to 0.232.
limitations: Three seeds; one dataset.

arxiv:2609.36059.title: Mnemon: Raw Records, Fast Judgments, Slow Thoughts
arxiv:2609.36059.relationship: Builds a memory agent in which hosted Jev 1.13 makes the fast judgments about raw records and an LLM plans and answers.
arxiv:2609.36059.summary: Keeps conversations as raw, dated records; an LLM writes searches and composes answers while Jev judges which returned records are needed, current or decisive, under explicit budgets.
arxiv:2609.36059.finding: Mnemon reached 91.7% on LoCoMo and 83.8% on LongMemEval-S from under 4k tokens of context per question (92.2% and 94.4% with a reasoning model as System 2); on the same records Jev separated gold evidence better than two LLMs (AUC 0.942 vs 0.900 and 0.853) at 3–11 times their speed.
caveats: No held-out benchmark: developed on the evaluation sets.
LLM graders; different graders from the comparison systems.

claims.headline: Memory agent: LoCoMo 91.7% with Jev judging evidence (AUC 0.94)
claims.text: With raw records and Jev judging retrieved evidence, Mnemon reached 91.7% on LoCoMo and 83.8% on LongMemEval-S from under 4k tokens per question; on the same records Jev separated gold evidence with AUC 0.942 against 0.900 and 0.853 for two LLMs, 3–11 times faster.
limitations: Benchmarks were not held out during development.

arxiv:2609.36115.title: Koa-action: Fast and Consistent Structured Decision Making with Generative LLMs
arxiv:2609.36115.relationship: Proposes single-token “atomic action” decisions from fine-tuned generative LLMs as an alternative to dedicated decision models, compared with Jev.
arxiv:2609.36115.summary: Adds atomic label tokens and fine-tunes open (multimodal) LLMs so classification, endpointing, Boolean checks and scoring become one deterministic decoding step, and evaluates latency and accuracy under production serving.
arxiv:2609.36115.task: Low-latency classification and intent routing, including multimodal inputs.
arxiv:2609.36115.finding: Koa-action reached 85.5% on intent routing, within 2 points of the strongest frontier models, at 0.53 s median (1.9–7.5× faster) with a flat tail across label-space sizes; the authors report it competitive with Jev on accuracy and faster at the median.
caveats: Industrial benchmark not public.
Jev comparison reported qualitatively in the abstract.

claims.headline: Single-token LLM classifier: 85.5% at 0.53 s, flat across label spaces
claims.text: A fine-tuned single-token generative classifier reached 85.5% on an intent-routing benchmark, within 2 points of the strongest frontier models, at 0.53 s median and 0.63 s p95, with medians within 3 ms of each other across very different label spaces.
limitations: Production data not released.

arxiv:2609.36116.title: Dyad: Extending Large Language Models with Native Typed Decision-Making
arxiv:2609.36116.relationship: Extends pretrained LLMs with a native typed-decision head (an action encoder scored against the LLM state), compared with hosted Jev 1.13 on JevBench.
arxiv:2609.36116.summary: Embeds each candidate action description in parallel with an environment-conditioned encoder and scores it against the LLM’s internal state, trained with reinforcement learning from environment interaction, with the LLM frozen or jointly trained.
arxiv:2609.36116.task: Agent action selection in interactive environments.
arxiv:2609.36116.finding: With the LLM frozen, training only the action encoder gave consistent gains on four unseen environments (up to 5.89 points on ALFWorld with GRPO); on JevBench, Dyad with reasoning reached 86.18% against Jev’s 85.01%.
caveats: Training pipeline not yet released.
JevBench comparison mixes reasoning and non-reasoning settings.

claims.headline: Native typed-decision head: 86.2% vs Jev 85.0% on JevBench
claims.text: On JevBench, Dyad with reasoning reached 86.18% overall accuracy against Jev’s 85.01%, with the largest advantage on the hard subset; on ALFWorld, adding the native decision head gave up to 5.89 points.
limitations: Reasoning enabled for Dyad; code not yet released.

arxiv:2609.36154.title: More Features Are Not More Evidence: Limits of Training-Free Human Activity Recognition with Jev
arxiv:2609.36154.relationship: Tests hosted jev-1.13.0 on training-free human activity recognition from textual descriptions of accelerometer signals.
arxiv:2609.36154.summary: Renders accelerometer windows as deterministic text (numbers, semantic qualifiers) and asks Jev to choose the activity, against a generative baseline and three supervised HAR models.
arxiv:2609.36154.finding: Jev stayed far below supervised recognition (best macro-F1 0.038, 0.118 and 0.089 across the three datasets); a semantic rendering of the numbers partly helped, and its probabilities were not reliably calibrated for recognition.
caveats: Representation and semantics change together.
Post-hoc fusion analysis did not replicate.

claims.headline: Sensor activity recognition from text: macro-F1 ≤ 0.12
claims.text: From textual descriptions of accelerometer windows, Jev’s best representation reached macro-F1 of only 0.038, 0.118 and 0.089 on WISDM, UCI341 and PAMAP2, far below supervised HAR models, and its probabilities were not reliably calibrated.
limitations: Interface (rendering) is part of the result.

arxiv:2609.36399.title: Calibrated to Whom? Persona and Language Effects on Cultural Values in JEV
arxiv:2609.36399.relationship: Audits the cultural values expressed by hosted jev-1.13.0 with the Values Survey Module 2013 under Saudi and American personas in English and Arabic.
arxiv:2609.36399.summary: Asks the 24 VSM 2013 items under 25 persona conditions, two languages and eight request formulations (288,000 answers) and compares the resulting Hofstede indices with human Saudi–US differences.
arxiv:2609.36399.finding: Answers were highly repeatable (ICC 0.997); without a persona they resembled Jev’s own American personas, and switching to Saudi personas reproduced 87% of the human Saudi–US difference in English but 62% in Arabic, with long-term orientation reversed.
caveats: One model version; one Arabic translation.
Hofstede scores from unmatched samples and periods.

code.note: Authors state prompts, responses and code will be released.
code.label: Not located

claims.headline: Persona shifts reproduce 87% (English) vs 62% (Arabic) of a human difference
claims.text: Switching personas from American to Saudi moved Jev’s VSM 2013 answers along the human Saudi–US difference by 87% of its size in English but only 62% in Arabic, with long-term orientation reversed; without a persona its answers resembled its American personas.
limitations: Hofstede references from unmatched samples.

arxiv:2609.36965.title: Chinese-Jev: Bringing System One Model to Chinese-Language Tasks
arxiv:2609.36965.relationship: Trains an open encoder-based Chinese typed-decision model and compares it with hosted Jev on a new Chinese benchmark.
arxiv:2609.36965.summary: Converts heterogeneous Chinese annotations into probability targets over candidate options, trains a light encoder to score candidates, adds domain fine-tuning and an INT8 on-device deployment, and introduces CJ-Bench (307,900 held-out decisions).
arxiv:2609.36965.task: Chinese-language general, medical, legal and financial decisions.
arxiv:2609.36965.finding: After pre-training, Chinese-Jev reached 69.20% on the general subset, slightly above hosted Jev (1.24% relative), and cut ECE from 11.45% to 3.78%; after domain fine-tuning it reached 92% of Jev’s average accuracy across three specialised domains at about 15 ms per decision.
caveats: Benchmark built by the authors.
No released weights or code located.

claims.headline: Language-specific open encoder ≈ hosted Jev in Chinese, better calibrated
claims.text: On CJ-Bench’s general subset, the open Chinese-Jev encoder reached 69.20% accuracy, 1.24% (relative) above hosted Jev, with ECE 3.78% against Jev’s 11.45%; across three specialised domains it reached 92% of Jev’s average accuracy at about 15 ms per decision.
limitations: Authors’ own benchmark.

arxiv:2609.37470.title: Probability Contracts: Accuracy, Coherence, and Decisions Across LLM Interfaces
arxiv:2609.37470.relationship: Benchmarks whether equivalent probability requests through different interfaces of hosted Jev and the open Kev lead to the same decisions.
arxiv:2609.37470.summary: Builds 1,000 finite worlds with exact posteriors and compares accuracy, interface coherence and failure-aware decisions across four model–interface configurations.
arxiv:2609.37470.task: Posterior probability reports and defer/act decisions across interfaces.
arxiv:2609.37470.finding: Kev had lower aggregate posterior error than Jev but larger complement and coarsening residuals; Jev’s Event and Choice interfaces chose different binary actions on 32.8% of valid pairs at a deferral cost of 0.10, and interface disagreement certified only 11–52% of the actual error.
caveats: Synthetic worlds with exact posteriors.
Two systems and four interfaces.

claims.headline: Two interfaces, same question: different decision on 32.8% of pairs
claims.text: Asking the same probability question through Jev’s Event and Choice interfaces changed the binary act/defer decision on 32.8% of valid pairs at a deferral cost of 0.10; disagreement between interfaces certified only 11–52% of mean pair error.
limitations: Synthetic worlds.

arxiv:2609.37647.title: Evaluating and Benchmarking the System One Model Jev
arxiv:2609.37647.relationship: Zero-shot evaluation of hosted jev-1.13.0 on 37 full evaluation splits against two open LLMs scored on identical requests.
arxiv:2609.37647.summary: Runs one frozen template per dataset (346,009 requests for under US$10) over classification, routing, NLI, reading comprehension, commonsense, moderation, legal clauses and rubric scoring, with Qwen3.8-27B and Gemma-4-E4B scored through their exact option probabilities.
datasets: 37 datasets incl. IMDB, SST-2, HellaSwag, ARC, MMLU, Belebele (122 languages), Banking77, ANLI, UNFAIR-ToS
arxiv:2609.37647.finding: Jev beat Qwen3.8-27B on 27 of 37 datasets (none of Qwen’s nine leads outside the intervals) and Gemma on all 37, with pooled Choice ECE 0.028; binary probabilities ranked well but sat poorly against a fixed 0.5 threshold (tuned thresholds raised UNFAIR-ToS micro-F1 from 0.50 to 0.75). Rotating options left accuracy unchanged, and calculation-heavy MMLU questions were easier for Jev than other MMLU questions (94% vs 91%).
caveats: One untuned template per dataset.
MMLU result may reflect memorised question–answer pairs.
All models degrade on low-resource languages and rubric judgments.

claims.headline: Ahead of a 27B open LLM on 27/37 datasets; pooled Choice ECE 0.028
claims.text: On identical requests, Jev scored higher than Qwen3.8-27B on 27 of 37 datasets (11 with non-overlapping intervals; none of Qwen’s nine leads) and higher than Gemma-4-E4B on all 37; pooled over 22 Choice datasets and 279,925 answers its ECE was 0.028.
limitations: One frozen template per dataset; open models scored via exact option probabilities.

claims.headline: Binary probabilities rank well; fixed 0.5 threshold does not
claims.text: Jev’s binary probabilities ranked well but were poorly placed against a fixed 0.5 threshold; thresholds tuned on training data raised UNFAIR-ToS micro-F1 from 0.50 to 0.75 and GoEmotions macro-F1 from 0.243 to 0.353.
limitations: Multi-label requests with rare labels.

claims.headline: Calculation-heavy MMLU easier for Jev (94% vs 91%) — memorisation not ruled out
claims.text: Calculation-heavy MMLU subjects were easier for Jev than its other subjects (94.3% vs 91.3%), the reverse of both open models (Qwen 74.7% vs 83.0%); withholding the question dropped MMLU accuracy to 31.5%, which rules out shallow memorisation but not memorised question–answer pairs.
limitations: Long-established English benchmark; possible contamination.

arxiv:2609.37832.title: Can a Cacheable Decision Model Follow Rules?
arxiv:2609.37832.relationship: Studies whether a small open non-generative decision model (Certo, Qwen3-4B) keeps rule sensitivity when candidates are encoded independently for caching.
arxiv:2609.37832.summary: Compares a joint scorer that reads state, rules and each candidate together with a cacheable independent encoder, and tests counterfactual supervision for restoring rule sensitivity.
arxiv:2609.37832.task: Rule-conditioned action scoring over candidate menus.
arxiv:2609.37832.finding: Converting to cacheable scoring cut rule-sensitive recall@1 from 1.00 to 0.24 while the joint scorer held 1.00 (about 5× more expensive at 77 candidates); counterfactual supervision restored held-out synthetic rule tasks, but on real rules the joint scorer kept its edge (0.861 vs 0.500 on the short tier).
caveats: Real-rule evaluations are small (tens of items per slice).
Paper does not compare with hosted Jev.

claims.headline: Cacheable scoring loses rule sensitivity (recall@1 1.00 → 0.24)
claims.text: Encoding candidates independently for caching cut rule-sensitive recall@1 from 1.00 to 0.24, while the joint scorer, which reads state, rules and candidate together, held 1.00 at a cost that grows with the menu; on real rules the joint scorer won 0.861 vs 0.500 on the short tier.
limitations: Small real-rule slices.

arxiv:2609.38827.title: More Choices, Fewer Decisions: Ordinal-Scale Bias in JEV-like Direct-Decision Models
arxiv:2609.38827.relationship: Shows that hosted Jev 1.13 and three open Kev models compress decisions on ordinal scales supplied by the user.
arxiv:2609.38827.summary: Measures how much of the effective gold support final decisions use across 36 ordinal and four nominal datasets, then refines scales on fixed items from K = 2 to 14 with balanced support and positions.
arxiv:2609.38827.task: Ordinal and nominal classification with user-supplied scales.
arxiv:2609.38827.finding: Jev reached 74.95% on ANLI yet assigned 38.8% of all predictions and 51.3% of its errors to Neutral, regardless of candidate position; across 36 ordinal datasets decisions used only 67–76% of effective gold support against 87–102% on nominal tasks, and utilisation fell as scales were refined from 2 to 14 levels.
caveats: Ordinal/nominal split is a binary taxonomy.
Same-item scaling covers three ordinal sources.

versions.note: Version string reported by the endpoint.

claims.headline: ANLI: Neutral absorbs 51% of errors, at every position
claims.text: On ANLI, Jev 1.13 reached 74.95% accuracy but assigned 38.8% of all predictions and 51.3% of its 1,603 errors to Neutral, selecting Neutral 37.2–39.6% of the time at every candidate position.
limitations: One dataset for the motivating case.

claims.headline: Ordinal scales compressed: decisions use 67–76% of gold support
claims.text: Across 36 ordinal datasets, final decisions used only 67–76% of the effective gold support against 87–102% on four nominal tasks; on fixed items with balanced support, utilisation fell as the scale was refined from 2 to 14 levels for every model.
limitations: Randomising candidate order weakens but does not remove the effect.

arxiv:2609.38850.title: OpenJev-RLCD: A Working RLCD Implementation
arxiv:2609.38850.relationship: Releases a working implementation of reinforcement learning for calibrated decisions (RLCD) for open reasoning models.
arxiv:2609.38850.summary: Samples a rationale, scores the answer distribution the model commits to with a strictly proper scoring rule, and uses a two-stage recipe (calibrate, then reinforce) after showing that the naive per-rationale objective switches reasoning off.
arxiv:2609.38850.task: Calibrated decisions on reasoning tasks with selective prediction.
arxiv:2609.38850.finding: With Qwen3-1.7B on two reasoning tasks, RLCD matched or beat SFT, RFT/STaR and GRPO in accuracy and beat all of them in selective prediction; when uncertainty comes from annotator disagreement, RLCD provably cannot beat cross-entropy.
caveats: 1.7B model, 400–800 steps, three seeds.
GSM8K-Verify built by the authors.

claims.headline: Open RLCD: best selective prediction among SFT, STaR, GRPO
claims.text: An open RLCD recipe (calibrate, then reinforce) on Qwen3-1.7B matched or beat SFT, RFT/STaR and GRPO in accuracy and beat all of them in selective prediction on two reasoning tasks; with annotator-disagreement uncertainty it cannot beat cross-entropy.
limitations: Small model; three seeds.

arxiv:2609.39111.title: Bongard: Training Machine Intuition
arxiv:2609.39111.relationship: Releases an open-weight System One model built on a T5Gemma 2 encoder–decoder with a trained judgment head.
arxiv:2609.39111.summary: Separates reading the state (a bidirectional encoder over state and question instructions) from judging (decoder branches sharing that encoding), returns probabilities over supplied candidates through a trained head, and trains in three stages: supervised judgments, semantic relationships (joint-embedding post-training) and action outcomes from sandbox rollouts with exact oracles.
arxiv:2609.39111.task: General typed decisions with several questions per state.
arxiv:2609.39111.finding: Joint-embedding post-training raised held-out rephrasing accuracy from 75.7% to 85.9% and the sandbox stage raised a frozen sandbox panel from 50.6% to 64.8%; the final model reached 78.05% on DecisionBench (fourth of 61 systems in the public comparison) with 36 ms median latency for short requests and 221 ms for 32 questions about one state on one RTX PRO 6000.
caveats: Leaderboard rank is a snapshot of a community benchmark.
The alignment stage is isolated only by a short control.
Weights under the Gemma terms of use, not an OSI licence.

claims.headline: Open encoder–decoder: 78.05% on DecisionBench, 32 questions in 221 ms
claims.text: The open-weight Bongard model reached 78.05% accuracy over 23,900 DecisionBench decisions (fourth of 61 systems in the public comparison of 29 September 2026); on one RTX PRO 6000 its median latency was 36 ms for short requests and 221 ms for 32 questions about one state.
limitations: Rank depends on the leaderboard snapshot.
Latency measured on the authors’ own GPU.

arxiv:2609.39496.title: When the Right Answer Is Missing: An Arithmetic-Dependent Rejection Bottleneck in Jev
arxiv:2609.39496.relationship: Shows that hosted Jev picks correct numerical answers when present but rarely rejects a menu that lacks one, even with an explicit “None” option.
arxiv:2609.39496.summary: Builds paired arithmetic problems in which the correct value is present or absent, varies magnitude, operation depth, context and rejection labels, extends to time calculation and capacity rounding, and compares menu Choice with native Boolean verification and a threshold rule.
arxiv:2609.39496.task: Rejecting candidate menus that contain no correct answer.
arxiv:2609.39496.finding: Answer-present accuracy reached 99% while correct rejection fell to 7%, a gap that persisted across magnitudes, depths, contexts and rejection labels; Boolean verification of the same candidates correctly rejected 99% of answer-absent cases, and a threshold chosen on separate development problems raised rejection to 79% while keeping 97% answer-present accuracy.
caveats: Hosted API only; mechanisms are inferred from inputs and outputs.
Synthetic arithmetic tasks.

versions.note: Version string reported in the paper.

claims.headline: Present 99%, rejected when absent 7% — though Boolean checks get 99%
claims.text: On paired arithmetic problems with an explicit “None” option, Jev chose the correct value 99% of the time when it was present but correctly rejected only 7% of menus where it was absent; native Boolean verification rejected all three wrong candidates on 99% of the same answer-absent cases.
limitations: Synthetic arithmetic; hosted API only.

claims.headline: Threshold from development data: rejection 7% → 79%
claims.text: A decision threshold selected on separate development problems raised correct rejection of answer-absent arithmetic menus from 7% to 79% while keeping 97% answer-present accuracy, without retraining or extra calls.
limitations: Threshold transfer beyond arithmetic not shown.

arxiv:2609.40241.title: Decision-Oriented Recommendation Reranking: An Empirical Study of Jev
arxiv:2609.40241.relationship: Controlled study of hosted Jev as a reranker of hard candidate sets for next-item recommendation.
arxiv:2609.40241.summary: Builds candidate sets from SASRec’s top-200 retrievals with the held-out next item and hard negatives, varies set size, and compares Jev with SASRec, DCNv2 and pointwise and listwise Qwen2.5-7B rerankers on NDCG@10, Hit Rate@10, MRR and observed serving latency.
datasets: Amazon Reviews 2023: Movies & TV (954 users), Video Games (1,000), Books (626)
arxiv:2609.40241.finding: Jev generally achieved the highest NDCG@10 on Video Games and Books and stayed strong as candidate sets grew, while its observed latency grew far more gradually than pointwise Qwen reranking but stayed well above SASRec and DCNv2.
caveats: Results reported mainly in figures.
Hosted latency includes network and gateway overhead; local baselines do not.
One decision model; larger LLM rerankers not tested.

versions.note: Moving alias; resolved version not reported.

claims.headline: Strong reranking quality; latency between local models and pointwise LLMs
claims.text: On hard candidate sets from three Amazon Reviews domains (2,580 users), Jev generally achieved higher NDCG@10 than SASRec, DCNv2 and Qwen2.5 rerankers on Video Games and Books; its observed latency grew much more slowly with set size than pointwise Qwen reranking but stayed well above the recommendation-specific models.
limitations: Hosted latency includes network overhead; local baselines run on one GPU.

arxiv:2610.00213.title: Counting the Uncounted: Population-Level Surveillance of Documented Pregnancy and Fetal Harm in Police Crash Narratives with a System One Model (Jev)
arxiv:2610.00213.relationship: Uses hosted Jev to read every Texas police crash narrative from 2017 to 2025 for documented pregnancy and fetal harm.
arxiv:2610.00213.summary: Screens 5,018,079 narratives with regular expressions, has Jev read the 6,840 flagged candidates under an eight-question schema and 499,306 of the remainder under the presence question, and corrects counts with blind human adjudication of a probability-stratified sample and a Rogan–Gladen estimator.
arxiv:2610.00213.task: Population-level public-health surveillance from police narratives.
arxiv:2610.00213.finding: Jev confirmed 5,333 narratives documenting a pregnant person; blind adjudication of a probability-stratified sample gave weighted sensitivity 0.999 and specificity 1.000, yielding an estimated 5,467 crashes with a documented pregnancy (95% interval 5,306–5,577), including 58 documenting fetal harm.
caveats: Narratives under a data agreement; not public.
Documentation is not occurrence: narratives record 2.56–3.09% of expected pregnant drivers.

code.note: Schema, runner, analysis scripts and adjudication tool (MIT).
code.label: Available

data.note: Police narratives under a data agreement.
data.label: Restricted

claims.headline: Population-scale reading audited by blind coders: sensitivity 0.999
claims.text: Reading 6,840 regex-flagged Texas crash narratives and 499,306 others, Jev confirmed 5,333 documenting a pregnant person; blind adjudication by two coders (Cohen’s κ 0.944) of a probability-stratified sample gave weighted sensitivity 0.999 and specificity 1.000, and the corrected estimate was 5,467 crashes (95% interval 5,306–5,577).
limitations: Same author team as other studies in this family.
Easy presence question on a pre-screened pool.

arxiv:2610.00346.title: Benchmarking System One decision models against trained classifiers and language models for automated decision gates
arxiv:2610.00346.relationship: Compares hosted Jev and open decision-model checkpoints with trained classifiers and generative models as automated decision gates under one harness.
arxiv:2610.00346.summary: Sends eight decision-model checkpoints from six families (hosted Jev pinned to jev-1.13.0; Laya, Kev, decider-2b, this-that-model and Nimble) and two generative comparators identical typed requests on a synthetic workflow benchmark, a 150-intent benchmark with out-of-scope inputs and four social-science tasks, with stress tests over option count, distractor permutations and yes/no swaps.
arxiv:2610.00346.task: Automated decision gates: accuracy, calibration transfer, robustness and cascades.
baselines: Two generative comparators via option-key likelihoods
arxiv:2610.00346.finding: The ranking of model classes depended on conditions: trained classifiers led on intents when labels existed, while most decision models beat zero-shot entailment without labels; a held-out threshold for 5% in-scope risk still let Jev accept 0.310 of out-of-scope requests, swapping yes and no flipped 50.5 of every 100 Jev answers, and an intent-trained first stage escalating to Jev matched its accuracy at 0.43 of its cost.
caveats: Same author team as other studies in this family.
Cost ratio assumes full GPU utilisation.
No code release located.

claims.headline: Threshold for 5% risk still admits 31% of out-of-scope requests
claims.text: A threshold chosen on held-out data for 5% in-scope risk still let Jev accept 0.310 of out-of-scope requests on the 150-intent benchmark, and temperatures fitted on few options raised calibration error when many options were offered.
limitations: One intent benchmark.

claims.headline: Yes/no swap flips half of the hosted model’s answers
claims.text: Swapping the meaning of yes and no against fixed rubrics flipped 50.5 of every 100 binary answers for hosted Jev, while fine-tuned open checkpoints cut their backbones’ flips on social-science items.
limitations: Rubric-based binary tasks.

claims.headline: Classifier first, Jev on escalation: same accuracy at 0.43 of the cost
claims.text: An intent-trained classifier as first stage, escalating uncertain inputs to Jev, matched Jev’s accuracy at 0.43 of its cost at full graphics-processor utilisation.
limitations: Cost depends on assumed GPU utilisation.

arxiv:2610.00376.title: A First Glance at Jev for Network Traffic Classification: Accuracy, Processing Time, and Cost
arxiv:2610.00376.relationship: First look at hosted Jev for application classification of QUIC flows from the first ten packets.
arxiv:2610.00376.summary: Gives Jev only the sizes, directions and inter-packet times of the first ten packets of each flow over 52,000 records from 26 collection weeks, with 0, 40 or 150 fixed labelled examples, against Random Forest and Extra Trees trained on 8,000 earlier records and, on a paired subset, a generative model.
arxiv:2610.00376.task: Ten-class application classification of encrypted network flows.
arxiv:2610.00376.finding: Zero-shot Jev reached 9.80% accuracy, below the 22.79% majority constant; 40 labelled examples raised it to 28.42% and 150 examples to 34.50% on the first test week, while tree ensembles trained on 8,000 records reached 69.95% and 66.80% and beat Jev in every week.
caveats: Unequal supervision budgets between Jev and the trees.
Fixed service configurations; raw responses not released.

versions.note: Version string reported by the endpoint.

data.note: Public dataset.
data.label: Available

predictions.note: Aggregate data and source hashes only.
predictions.label: Not located

claims.headline: Packet numbers in, 28% accuracy out — trees trained on 8k records reach 70%
claims.text: Given only the first ten packets’ sizes, directions and timings, Jev classified 9.80% of 52,000 QUIC flows correctly zero-shot (below a 22.79% majority constant) and 28.42% with 40 labelled examples; Random Forest and Extra Trees trained on 8,000 records reached 69.95% and 66.80% and beat Jev in every one of 26 weeks.
limitations: Unequal supervision budgets.

claims.headline: 0.75 s vs 6.0 s per request; accuracy difference not established
claims.text: On a paired 100-record subset, Jev with 40 examples reached 29% accuracy at a median request time of 0.750 s against 37% and 6.036 s for GPT-5.6 Sol with high reasoning effort through Azure; the subset does not establish an accuracy advantage for either service.
limitations: 100 records; different service configurations.

arxiv:2610.00381.title: OmniMed-Jev: Calibrating LVLM Confidence for Trustworthy Medical Multimodal Decisions via System One
arxiv:2610.00381.relationship: Trains a medical multimodal model to output decision distributions (Choice, binary and bounded Score) over runtime-supplied candidates and compares it with a generative twin.
arxiv:2610.00381.summary: Adds a shared candidate-conditioned decision head to a MedGemma-1.5-4B backbone and trains it against a generative baseline with the same backbone, data and schedule across four task families drawn from fifteen public imaging datasets.
arxiv:2610.00381.task: Medical image classification, multi-label findings, counting and regression with calibrated outputs.
datasets: Fifteen public medical imaging datasets (histology, CT, dermatology, ophthalmology, chest X-ray, ultrasound and others)
baselines: Generative twin on the same backbone, data and schedule
arxiv:2610.00381.finding: The decision-native model’s probabilities tracked correctness far more closely, cutting calibration error by up to an order of magnitude and reliability error by up to two orders, while point predictions stayed comparable; counting was the one family where the generative baseline stayed ahead.
caveats: Interface and associated training differences cannot be separated.
Retrospective benchmarks; not evidence of clinical readiness.

data.note: Public de-identified datasets.
data.label: Available

claims.headline: Same backbone, decision-native output: calibration error down up to 10×
claims.text: Against a generative baseline with the same backbone, data and schedule, the decision-distribution model cut calibration error by up to an order of magnitude and reliability error by up to two orders across medical imaging tasks, with comparable point predictions; counting was the exception.
limitations: Interface and training differences confounded.
Not clinical validation.

arxiv:2610.00437.title: JevSpawn: Adaptive Agentic Inference through Compositional Action Spaces
arxiv:2610.00437.relationship: Agent policy that derives finite action spaces from natural-language task specifications and explores them with Jev-style scoring.
arxiv:2610.00437.summary: Spawns parallel candidate actions, selects branches from feedback, revises the action representation and recovers from retained alternatives, sharing action structure and model prefixes; compares open Qwen scoring with a hosted Jev variant inside the same architecture.
arxiv:2610.00437.task: Puzzle and navigation tasks requiring multi-step exploration.
datasets: Eight tasks: Maze, Grid, PPNL, LightsOut, Sokoban, RushHour, 2048, Nullify
arxiv:2610.00437.finding: JevSpawn reached success rates of 0.96 and 0.95 on Maze and Grid (FoldAgent 0.52 and 0.73) and cut end-to-end latency there from 47.91 and 61.44 s to about 41 s; inside the same architecture hosted Jev beat Qwen scoring on three tasks, matched one and trailed on four, and took 1.4–2.1 times as long including API communication.
caveats: Puzzle environments.
Hosted variant timing includes network communication.

claims.headline: Agent with spawned finite actions: Maze 0.96 vs 0.52
claims.text: With compositional action spawning, success rates reached 0.96 on Maze and 0.95 on Grid against 0.52 and 0.73 for FoldAgent, while end-to-end latency fell from the fastest baselines’ 47.91 and 61.44 s to 40.91 and 40.58 s; on LightsOut and 2048 higher scores came with longer runs.
limitations: Gains come from the whole policy, not only the scorer.

claims.headline: Hosted Jev inside the agent: better on 3 of 8 tasks, 1.4–2.1× slower
claims.text: Swapping the finite scorer inside JevSpawn for hosted Jev improved PPNL, LightsOut (0.66 vs 0.61) and Sokoban, matched Maze and lowered Grid, RushHour, 2048 and Nullify, and took 1.4–2.1 times as long as local Qwen scoring across all eight tasks including API communication.
limitations: Hosted timing includes network round trips.

arxiv:2610.00831.title: AnyJev Technical Report
arxiv:2610.00831.relationship: Reads typed decisions from one prefill of any instruction-tuned language model and removes label and position biases without training.
arxiv:2610.00831.summary: Restricts the next-token distribution at the answer position to option tokens, divides out a label prior estimated from unlabelled inputs, averages log-probabilities over cyclic rotations of the option list, and adds a stopping rule that reads fewer rotations with a bounded disagreement.
arxiv:2610.00831.task: Typed decisions from off-the-shelf language models.
arxiv:2610.00831.finding: Reversing the option list changed the answer on about 33% of items averaged over eleven models; rotation averaging lowered the order-flip rate on two 20-option tasks from 0.33 to 0.14 and 0.18 and raised accuracy for 11 of 11 models on both, and the stopping rule served 2.2 times as many decisions per second on vLLM.
caveats: One prefill cannot reason: hardest JevBench tier spans 0.343–0.590.
JevBench items average 3.6 options, where rotation helps least.

claims.headline: Order flips on a third of 20-option items; rotation averaging halves them
claims.text: Across eleven open models, reversing the option list changed the argmax on 32.8% of banking20 and 33.4% of newsgroups items; averaging over cyclic rotations cut the order-flip rate to 0.14 and 0.18 and raised accuracy for 11 of 11 models on both tasks, at the cost of one prefill per rotation.
limitations: Open models only; hosted Jev not tested.

arxiv:2610.01006.title: Beyond Answer Confidence: A Controlled Audit of Self-Knowledge in a Black-Box Decision Model
arxiv:2610.01006.relationship: Controlled audit of whether hosted Jev’s confidence signals missing knowledge, not just chance.
arxiv:2610.01006.summary: Uses more than 15 public datasets and six generated task families with paired interventions that vary the information supplied for a fixed item (chance events, removed evidence, fabricated entities, news beyond a knowledge boundary), and compares answer confidence with targeted yes/no questions.
arxiv:2610.01006.task: Self-knowledge and abstention signals in a black-box decision model.
datasets: 15+ public datasets (incl. Banking77 subset, CLINC150, Quizbowl)
arxiv:2610.01006.finding: Jev was calibrated on familiar closed-choice tasks but its confidence failed as a missing-knowledge signal: with no answer-relevant information it put up to 0.80 on a salient option, and on news beyond its knowledge boundary confidence exceeded accuracy by 0.21–0.33 even after recalibration on earlier months; targeted yes/no questions on whether an outcome is settled (AUROC 1.00) or evidence suffices (0.95 vs 0.85) worked better, while “do you know?” questions mostly tracked surface cues.
caveats: One version of one closed model.
Follow-up questions evaluated on curated contrasts.

claims.headline: Confidence ≠ knowing: +0.21–0.33 overconfidence past the knowledge boundary
claims.text: With no answer-relevant information Jev still assigned up to 0.80 to a salient option, and on news beyond an observed knowledge boundary its confidence exceeded accuracy by 0.21–0.33, a gap that recalibration on earlier months did not close.
limitations: Generated and curated interventions.

claims.headline: Ask the model a targeted question instead of reading its confidence
