claims.text: Asking targeted yes/no questions separated cases better than answer confidence: whether an outcome is settled reached AUROC 1.00 and whether evidence suffices 0.95 against 0.85 for confidence; asking whether Jev knows the answer reached 0.91 but lost its advantage with realistic names or dates removed.
limitations: Surface cues explain much of the knowledge-question signal.

arxiv:2610.01079.title: Jev-IDS: System One Models for Network Intrusion Detection
arxiv:2610.01079.relationship: Open experimental network intrusion detector that asks hosted Jev for an attack probability and a traffic category per flow under label scarcity.
arxiv:2610.01079.summary: Serialises one flow per request with one or two labelled examples per category and asks two typed questions; compares Jev with GPT-5.6 Luna and a low-data Random Forest over three seeds, including categories unseen in the examples.
arxiv:2610.01079.task: Zero-day intrusion detection with scarce labels.
arxiv:2610.01079.finding: At one example per category Jev was 4.8 times faster and 3.8 times cheaper than GPT-5.6 Luna with 1.5 times higher novel-attack recall, and raised 15 times fewer false alarms than the low-data Random Forest; across 5,400 decisions it reached F1 0.859 (precision 0.941, recall 0.790), and two examples lowered F1 to 0.839.
caveats: 300-flow pilot on a historical dataset.
Low-data Random Forest is a weak reference.

claims.headline: Intrusion pilot: F1 0.859, 4.8× faster than an LLM
claims.text: On a 300-flow NSL-KDD pilot (5,400 decisions), Jev reached F1 0.859 with one example per category, was 4.8 times faster and 3.8 times cheaper than GPT-5.6 Luna with 1.5 times higher novel-attack recall, and raised 15 times fewer false alarms than a Random Forest trained on the same examples.
limitations: Small pilot; historical dataset.

arxiv:2610.01601.title: Permutation-Robust Decision Modeling with Candidate-Independent Block-Causal Attention
arxiv:2610.01601.relationship: Proposes block-causal attention that isolates candidates from one another so open decision models score options independently of their order.
arxiv:2610.01601.summary: Keeps causal attention within the shared context and each candidate, blocks attention across candidates and resets candidate positions; trains matched models on the Open-Jev data with Gemma 3 1B, Qwen3 1.7B and Qwen3 4B backbones against causal and invariant baselines, with ablations.
arxiv:2610.01601.finding: Candidate isolation cut test permutation flip rates from 8.3% to 0.1% (Gemma 3 1B), 18.2% to 1.2% (Qwen3 1.7B) and 7.2% to 0.7% (Qwen3 4B) while keeping competitive accuracy (84.96% vs 81.84% on Qwen3 1.7B); isolation was the main source of the effect and position resetting completed it.
caveats: Single author; open backbones up to 4B.
Dual-encoder comparison not optimisation-matched.

data.note: Open-Jev dataset.
data.label: Available

claims.headline: Isolate candidates: order flips 18.2% → 1.2%
claims.text: Blocking attention between candidates and resetting their positions cut test permutation flip rates from 8.3% to 0.1% (Gemma 3 1B), 18.2% to 1.2% (Qwen3 1.7B) and 7.2% to 0.7% (Qwen3 4B) with competitive accuracy; isolation alone reduced flips to 3.82% and position reset alone made them worse (12.16%).
limitations: Open backbones only.

arxiv:2610.01834.title: Code Owns the Simulation, Jev Owns the Evaluation
arxiv:2610.01834.relationship: Locates a sharp boundary in hosted Jev’s use as an agent’s action selector: it evaluates what the input describes but does not simulate what it leaves out.
arxiv:2610.01834.summary: Tests Jev on Cognitive Reflection Test questions, one-shot matrix games, the ALFWorld text game and robot control, splitting decisions that need only evaluation of described options from those that need simulation (an opponent’s move, a subgoal that must come first), and then supplies the simulation from code.
arxiv:2610.01834.task: Action selection for agents: reflection tests, games, text games and robot control.
arxiv:2610.01834.finding: Jev answered 99% of Cognitive Reflection Test questions correctly but played games as if a rational opponent moved at random; stating the opponent’s action raised accuracy from 33% to 98%, a two-call decomposition reached 94%, and a code lookahead raised ALFWorld games solved from 31% to 87%.
caveats: Single model version; hand-built decompositions.
No code release located.

claims.headline: Evaluates what is described; does not simulate what is not
claims.text: Jev solved 99% of Cognitive Reflection Test questions (95% interval 0.97–1.00) but in one-shot games chose as if a rational opponent acted at random; asked separately, it predicted the opponent’s action 90% of the time and played the best response 98% of the time once that action was stated (33% → 98%).
limitations: Curated games and questions.

claims.headline: Let code simulate: ALFWorld solved 31% → 87%
claims.text: In ALFWorld, Jev alone solved 31% of 134 games, favouring commands that mention objects named in the task; with a code-supplied lookahead it solved 87%, and with physics simulation from code it became an effective robot controller.
limitations: Lookahead uses a copy of the environment.

arxiv:2610.02046.title: Prune First, Decide Fast: Scalable Semantic Query Processing with JEVDB
arxiv:2610.02046.relationship: Semantic database engine that runs filters, joins, classification and ranking on fast typed decision models and escalates uncertain cases to generative LLMs.
arxiv:2610.02046.summary: Combines exact semijoin reduction with Semantic Bloom Filters built from registered necessary conditions, evaluates the remaining pairs with Jev in parallel, and sends cases whose calibrated uncertainty exceeds an error threshold to a generative model.
arxiv:2610.02046.task: Semantic SQL query processing over unstructured data.
datasets: Shelob (TPC-DS-derived semantic joins, up to 540K candidate pairs)
baselines: LLM-based semantic database systems on SemBench
arxiv:2610.02046.finding: On SemBench the Flash configuration had the lowest latency on all 21 queries and the lowest cost on 19 with competitive quality; on Shelob it completed every query with 95.7–97.5% mean F1 where baselines timed out, Semantic Bloom Filters removed 87.4% of candidate pairs before evaluation and reusable condition scoring cut escalations by 55.2%.
caveats: Authors’ own benchmark for joins.
Gains combine pruning, batching and the decision model.

code.note: The paper points to the project site, which hosts an interactive simulator; no public source repository was located.
code.label: Claimed, not located

claims.headline: Semantic SQL: pruning + typed decisions finish 540K-pair joins
claims.text: JEVDB-Flash had the lowest latency on all 21 SemBench queries and the lowest cost on 19; on Shelob joins with up to 540K candidate pairs it finished every query at 95.7–97.5% mean F1, with Semantic Bloom Filters pruning 87.4% of pairs and condition-index scoring cutting reasoning-model escalations by 55.2%.
limitations: System gains mix pruning and model choice.

arxiv:2610.02048.title: HydroJEV: A one-second, training-free screen for cyber-attack and fault attribution in water distribution networks
arxiv:2610.02048.relationship: Tests hosted Jev as a training-free first tier for attributing SCADA alarms in water distribution networks.
arxiv:2610.02048.summary: Builds a four-class cause-attribution benchmark (cyberattack, physical fault, normal transient, faulty sensor) on the C-Town network in EPANET and compares Jev with a rule tree, a supervised classifier and seven cloud LLMs on identical evidence over four sealed, pre-registered rounds, then transfers an agreement-gated cascade to two further networks.
arxiv:2610.02048.task: Cause attribution of anomaly alarms in water networks.
datasets: C-Town (EPANET) simulated windows, four sealed rounds
arxiv:2610.02048.finding: With only a label-free prior correction, Jev matched the rule tree in distribution (macro-F1 0.62–0.64 vs 0.56–0.61), beat the supervised classifier by 0.36–0.42 on event subtypes absent from its labels in all four rounds, and decided 20–40 times faster than frontier LLMs; accepting only benign Jev verdicts confirmed by the rule tree spared an LLM reviewer 35–38% of windows without loss of macro-F1.
caveats: All windows simulated with one hydraulic model.
LLM timings from one client at one time.

data.note: Simulated windows and responses with the code.
data.label: Available

claims.headline: Pre-registered gate: a third of SCADA reviews offloaded, accuracy kept
claims.text: In four sealed, pre-registered rounds, accepting only benign Jev verdicts confirmed by a rule tree spared an LLM reviewer 35–38% of windows with no loss of macro-F1, and the unchanged cascade stayed within the non-inferiority margin of its reviewer on two further networks.
limitations: Simulated events.

claims.headline: No labels needed: beats a supervised classifier on unseen subtypes
claims.text: Jev matched a hand-written rule tree in distribution (macro-F1 0.62–0.64 vs 0.56–0.61) and exceeded a supervised classifier by 0.36–0.42 macro-F1 on event subtypes absent from the classifier’s labels in all four rounds, outperforming it whenever fewer than about four labelled events per class were available.
limitations: Simulated events; prior correction needed.

arxiv:2610.02076.title: LLM-as-Jev: LLMs Are Already Jev-Style Decision Models -- When and How to Fine-Tune Them
arxiv:2610.02076.relationship: Shows that instruction-tuned LLMs already work as Jev-style decision models when read through bracketed numeric identifiers, and studies when fine-tuning helps.
arxiv:2610.02076.summary: Scores candidates by next-token probabilities over bracketed numeric identifiers after the full candidate slate, and fine-tunes with a tree-factorised listwise loss plus KL anchors that keep other generation behaviour unchanged; evaluated on Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3-0.6B.
arxiv:2610.02076.task: Typed decisions from general LLMs, with and without fine-tuning.
baselines: Community Jev-style models on the same backbone (SemIf, Plumb, Hopper, reflex)
arxiv:2610.02076.finding: Frozen Qwen3.5-4B resolved 188 of 231 public JevBench items (81.4%), matching community models built on the same backbone, handled all 77 Banking77 intents in one pass (69.0%) and reached 82.4% on MMBench with images; fine-tuning helped the 0.6B model and many-option routing most, and LoRA with KL anchors gave the best 4B model (84.0%, ECE 0.050).
caveats: Public JevBench items only (231).
Two backbones from one family.

claims.headline: A frozen 4B LLM already matches community Jev-style models
claims.text: Without training, Qwen3.5-4B read through bracketed numeric identifiers resolved 188 of 231 public JevBench items (81.4%), matching or exceeding community Jev-style models on the same backbone (SemIf 186), and generating greedily picked the same candidate on all 231 items; LoRA with KL anchors raised it to 84.0% with ECE 0.050.
limitations: Small public item set.

arxiv:2610.02267.title: Fast Models, Slow Evidence: A Paired and Self-Audited Evaluation of System-1 Decision Models for LLM Agent Harnesses
arxiv:2610.02267.relationship: Paired evaluation of hosted Jev and the open Laya at eleven agent-harness decision points, with an audit of the authors’ own analysis.
arxiv:2610.02267.summary: Builds 11 decision points (model routing to PII egress) from 18 public sources, 7,283 base cases plus 6,640 robustness variants, with byte-identical inputs, paired tests and cross-hardware and cross-day reproducibility checks, then audits which of its own headline deployment claims survive.
arxiv:2610.02267.task: Typed decisions inside LLM agent harnesses.
datasets: 11 decision points from 18 public sources (7,283 base cases, 6,640 variants)
arxiv:2610.02267.finding: Jev was significantly more accurate on 9 of 11 decision points (+10.8 to +46.0 pp); neither beat chance on zero-shot model routing and they tied on RAG relevance gating. Laya changed 30% of answers when options were reversed and fell to 31% with 50 near-duplicate tools against 98% for Jev. The self-audit found that an omitted pre-screen cost turned a reported 23.9% saving into 4.3%, gate accuracy had been reported as end-to-end quality (58% vs 98%), and in-sample thresholds aimed at 5% misses gave up to 17% on held-out data.
caveats: Single versions, zero-shot, English-dominant public data.
About 5 pp wording band on absolute accuracies.

code.note: Cases, raw outputs and analysis code.
code.label: Available

claims.headline: Hosted beats open on 9 of 11 harness decisions; routing at chance for both
claims.text: On byte-identical inputs, Jev was significantly more accurate than the open Laya on 9 of 11 agent-harness decision points (+10.8 to +46.0 pp); neither beat chance on zero-shot model routing, and Laya changed 30% of its answers when the option order was reversed and fell to 31% with 50 near-duplicate tools against 98% for Jev.
limitations: Zero-shot, single versions.

claims.headline: Self-audit: a 23.9% saving was really 4.3%
claims.text: Auditing its own pipeline, the study found that omitting the pre-screen cost turned a reported 23.9% saving into 4.3%, gate accuracy had been reported as end-to-end quality (58% vs 98%), and thresholds tuned in-sample for 5% misses gave up to 17% misses on held-out data.
limitations: Savings depend on unobserved production base rates.

claims.headline: Hosted answers drift day to day (0.5%); open model reproduces exactly
claims.text: Repeating 1,080 decisions one day later changed 5 of Jev’s answers (0.5%), while the open Laya reproduced 1,180 of 1,180 decisions bit-for-bit on a second machine.
limitations: One-day interval.

arxiv:2610.02293.title: HakemBench: A Turkish Benchmark of Typed Decisions
arxiv:2610.02293.relationship: Open Turkish benchmark of typed decisions with a scorer for decision quality, calibration and selective automation.
arxiv:2610.02293.summary: Releases 2,346 items and 4,275 choice, yes/no and score questions in seven tracks under CC BY 4.0, with gold mostly from blind passes of one AI model family checked against a panel of other LLMs, a composite of macro-F1, normalised Brier and risk–coverage area, and probes for option order, paraphrase, translation and names.
arxiv:2610.02293.task: Turkish typed decisions across seven applied tracks.
baselines: 16-row board incl. Gemini 3.8 Flash, GPT-5.6 Sol, GLM 5.3, Kev, Laya, open-jev
arxiv:2610.02293.finding: Three hosted chat models and Jev 1.13 led the 16-row board (composites 0.825–0.888); Jev ranked fourth at 0.825 with a median of 135 ms against 1,294 ms for the leader. The lab’s own model ranked seventh (0.660), and its numbers are not blind because earlier test results shaped its training data.
caveats: Gold labels mostly AI-made and not human-verified; one human annotator.
The benchmark’s authors also build a ranked model.

data.note: CC BY 4.0.
data.label: Available

claims.headline: Turkish typed decisions: Jev fourth of 16 at a tenth of the leader’s time
claims.text: On HakemBench’s 16-row board, Gemini 3.8 Flash led with a composite of 0.888 and Jev 1.13 ranked fourth at 0.825 (0.811–0.837) with a median of 135 ms per item against 1,294 ms for the leader; the benchmark authors’ own model ranked seventh (0.660), and its numbers are flagged as not blind.
limitations: AI-made gold; authors also rank their own model.

arxiv:2610.02486.title: From Retrieval to Typed Decisions: Calibrated System One Models from Biomedical Sentence Encoders
arxiv:2610.02486.relationship: Converts biomedical sentence encoders trained for retrieval into calibrated typed-decision models and compares heads and training objectives.
arxiv:2610.02486.summary: Turns Sentence-Transformers encoders into bi-encoder, cross-head and prior-fused residual (PFR) decision models, introduces the BIODECIDE suite and MEDLINE-S1 (243k training decisions from NLM indexing), and compares cross-entropy, proper scoring rules and the released RLCD recipe of open System One models.
arxiv:2610.02486.task: Biomedical typed decisions from encoder models.
arxiv:2610.02486.finding: Retrieval training helped zero-shot matching and helped the PFR head in 10 of 15 fine-tuned comparisons but helped the cross head in one and hurt it in five; the cross head beat PFR under every objective, and the released RLCD recipe trailed cross-entropy by 2.5–3.0 points because its reward normalisation inflated a noisy gradient term 3.6–15-fold.
caveats: Base-size encoders and one training budget.
Parent–retriever pairs share parents; not independent replications.

data.note: MEDLINE-S1 labels.
data.label: Available

claims.headline: Open RLCD recipe trails plain cross-entropy by 2.5–3.0 points
claims.text: In a matched grid of heads and objectives on biomedical encoders, the released RLCD recipe of open System One models trailed cross-entropy by 2.5–3.0 points, mainly because its reward normalisation inflated the noisy score-function term 3.6–15-fold; an unbiased leave-one-out estimator recovered most of the gap, and after temperature scaling no objective was clearly better calibrated than cross-entropy.
limitations: One encoder for the objective grid.

arxiv:2610.02586.title: Labels Override Definitions in Jev-Style Typed Decision Models
arxiv:2610.02586.relationship: Shows in open Jev-style models that the probability follows short option labels rather than the written definitions, and locates the cause in prompt rendering.
arxiv:2610.02586.summary: Tests four open-weight typed-decision models and three readouts of a Qwen2.5 backbone on eleven classification tasks and PolicyBench, a synthetic routing suite in which the rule appears only in the definitions, then patches the one expression that renders options and gives a two-call diagnostic test.
arxiv:2610.02586.task: Whether typed decisions follow option definitions or labels.
arxiv:2610.02586.finding: Deleting every definition left laya-td accuracy unchanged (0.8559 vs 0.8487) although definitions alone supported 0.7971, and renaming options to A and B raised routing accuracy by 0.151; rendering options without the label made all three laya checkpoints exactly invariant, while adding labels created the effect in von, whose accuracy fell from 0.8511 to 0.2281 when a label contradicted its definition.
caveats: Hosted Jev not measured.
PolicyBench is synthetic and templated.

claims.headline: The label wins over the definition — and the cause is one rendering line
claims.text: In open typed-decision models the answer mostly followed option labels: deleting definitions left laya-td unchanged (0.8559 vs 0.8487), renaming options to A and B gained 0.151 accuracy, and one changed rendering line made laya exactly invariant while a contradicting label dropped von from 0.8511 to 0.2281.
limitations: Open-weight models only.

arxiv:2610.03073.title: SecJev: Bringing Security Expertise to System One Decision Models
arxiv:2610.03073.relationship: Family of Jev-like decision models specialised for security, built on Kev’s single-pass candidate scorer.
arxiv:2610.03073.summary: Builds SecJev-Corpus (14 tasks from eight sources: tool outputs, traffic, federated updates, consensus, authentication and vehicle messages) to unify source-label prediction and explicit-policy evaluation, and trains 0.8B–9B models with scene-weighted LoRA adapters and a pointer head.
arxiv:2610.03073.task: Security decisions from text, telemetry and observation histories.
arxiv:2610.03073.finding: Security specialisation improved every model in the family: SecJev-0.8B gained 39.40 points of task-macro accuracy over Kev-0.8B and beat general Kev-9B by 20.51 points, with accuracy and latency close to answer-only generative fine-tuning at lower peak memory; gains over Kev held on new prompt-injection and traffic sources, with capture-dependent false alarms.
caveats: Tasks measure source-label prediction and displayed-rule application, not end-to-end defence.
Uneven task sizes.

code.note: Adapters, decision heads, corpus and code.
code.label: Available

data.note: Source-specific terms preserved (e.g. academic-use conditions).
data.label: Partial

claims.headline: Security-specialised 0.8B beats general 9B by 20.5 points
claims.text: Specialising Kev’s candidate scorer on 14 security tasks raised SecJev-0.8B’s task-macro accuracy by 39.40 points over Kev-0.8B and 20.51 points above general Kev-9B, with accuracy and latency close to answer-only generative fine-tuning at lower peak memory.
limitations: Specialised vs general comparison within one family.

arxiv:2610.03324.title: To Jev or Not? Evaluating the Accuracy and Efficiency of Structured Decision Models for Hate-Speech Moderation
arxiv:2610.03324.relationship: Evaluates hosted and open decision models for hate-speech moderation against moderation models, zero-shot classifiers, commercial LLMs and supervised classifiers.
arxiv:2610.03324.summary: Runs six decision-model configurations (jev-1.13.0, Laya, Decider, SemIf with two backbones, Bespoke-Nimble-9B) on four hate-speech datasets with and without dataset definitions and with definition-specific decomposition, measuring macro-F1, latency and cost.
arxiv:2610.03324.finding: Commercial LLMs significantly beat all decision models on only one of four datasets (by 4.1–5.9 macro-F1), and supervised classifiers lost up to 54 points out of distribution; supplying definitions changed up to 28% of predictions but improved agreement in only 29% of comparisons, decomposition helped in 20% and hurt in 37%, and the best hosted decision model came within 1.6 points of the best commercial LLM at about 97% lower inference cost.
caveats: Definitions differ across datasets.
No code release located.

claims.headline: Definitions move 28% of answers — without reliably improving them
claims.text: Supplying a dataset’s hate-speech definition changed up to 28% of a decision model’s predictions but significantly improved agreement with annotations in only 29% of model–dataset comparisons and reduced it in as many; decomposing the definition into several questions helped in 20% and hurt in 37%.
limitations: Four datasets with different definitions.

claims.headline: Within 1.6 macro-F1 of the best LLM at ~97% lower cost
claims.text: Commercial LLMs significantly outperformed all decision models on only one of four hate-speech datasets, and on a diagnostic set the best hosted decision model came within 1.6 macro-F1 points of the best commercial LLM at about 97% lower inference cost.
limitations: Cost comparison at list prices.

arxiv:2610.03387.title: Benchmarking candidate coverage and rejection policy transfer in typed decision models
arxiv:2610.03387.relationship: Paired benchmark protocol for whether typed decision models notice that the reference answer is missing from the supplied options.
arxiv:2610.03387.summary: Compares Laya, hosted Jev and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on missing-answer detection and false rejection: tests whether rejection thresholds calibrated on one task transfer to others at equal calibration budgets, and separates artificial omission, natural retrieval misses and out-of-scope queries on CLINC150; an earlier discovery stage on AG News, DBpedia, Emotion and TREC is kept in the appendix.
arxiv:2610.03387.task: Rejection when the reference answer is missing from the candidate set, and transfer of rejection policies across tasks and candidate configurations.
datasets: CLINC150 (artificial omission, BM25 retrieval misses, out-of-scope queries)
arxiv:2610.03387.finding: Rejection thresholds calibrated on one task often failed on another: with 80 calibration pairs, none-score policies exceeded 5% target false rejection in six of twelve transfers for both Laya and Jev, a Jev policy fitted on DBpedia rejected 69.3% of covered Emotion inputs and an Emotion-fitted policy disabled rejection; with retrieved CLINC150 menus, more candidates raised Laya’s out-of-scope detection to 99.0% at 48.8% false rejection while Jev kept about 3% false rejection but detected 75.0%.
caveats: One checkpoint or version per model; natural-miss estimates rest on few cases at larger candidate counts.
Discovery-stage results (TREC native rejection) are kept separately in the appendix.

code.note: Benchmark code, frozen requests, recorded predictions and scoring outputs.
code.label: Available

data.note: Reconstruction indices for pinned public sources.
data.label: Available

claims.headline: Rejection thresholds do not travel: 69% false rejection after transfer
claims.text: With 80 calibration pairs per source task, none-score rejection policies exceeded 5% target false rejection in six of twelve task transfers for each of Laya and Jev; a Jev policy calibrated on DBpedia rejected 69.3% of covered Emotion test inputs, and an Emotion-calibrated Jev policy disabled rejection entirely until it was recalibrated on target labels.
limitations: Two ordinary candidates and natural names in the transfer matrix.

claims.headline: More candidates: Laya rejects half of covered queries, Jev misses a quarter of out-of-scope ones
claims.text: On CLINC150 with BM25-retrieved menus, raising the candidate count from two to ten raised Laya’s out-of-scope detection from 83.0% to 99.0% and its false rejection of covered queries from 15.2% to 48.8%, while Jev kept false rejection near 3% but its out-of-scope detection fell from 84.0% to 75.0% (Qwen2.5-7B: 85.0% to 63.0%); with artificial omission at five candidates, Jev detected 63.7% of missing answers.
limitations: Natural-miss estimates at ten candidates rest on five cases.

claims.headline: Missing answer noticed 24.8% of the time (Jev) — Laya over-rejects
claims.text: With five TREC candidates and natural names, Jev detected only 24.8% of cases where the reference answer had been removed while falsely rejecting no present controls; Laya detected 97.2% but falsely rejected 69.7%; calibration-only thresholds moved Jev to 45.0% detection at 1.8% false rejection.
limitations: Small samples; four English tasks.

arxiv:2610.03935.title: General Decision Models: Benchmarking and Insights Beyond Jev
arxiv:2610.03935.relationship: Bilingual benchmark of general decision models against generative LLMs, with system-level tests and an open self-distilled decision model.
arxiv:2610.03935.summary: Builds JEVal (11,257 instances from 36 datasets in 10 domains, English and Chinese), evaluates 25 configurations, probes exact computation and probability estimation, long inputs, τ-bench tool agents and large-scale social simulation, and distils an open LLM’s reasoning into a single first-token decision (InnerJev-4B and -27B).
arxiv:2610.03935.task: General decision models across domains, agents and social simulation.
baselines: Thinking and non-thinking open LLMs (Qwen, DeepSeek, GLM)
Open decision models (Kev, Laya, Decider, Nimble)
arxiv:2610.03935.finding: The strongest decision models came within three points of leading thinking LLMs overall but fell behind on specialist knowledge; Jev picked the mode on all 100 prior-probability items yet put 89.35% of the mass on it against 35.60% in the true distribution; in τ-bench, Jev action selection cut median episode time from 267 s to 161 s but lowered success from 77.6% to 66.1%; InnerJev-27B performed on par with Jev at about 0.1 s per query.
caveats: Two agentic settings only.
InnerJev is the authors’ own model.

data.note: JEVal.
data.label: Available

claims.headline: Right mode, wrong mass: 89% placed where the truth is 36%
claims.text: On four-option items with analytically known distributions, Jev picked the most likely option on all 100 prior items and 67 posterior items, ahead of every non-thinking LLM, but placed 89.35% of the probability on the prior mode against 35.60% in the true distribution — the largest probability error of all configurations.
limitations: Synthetic probability tasks (100 items each).

claims.headline: Faster steps, slower agent: success 77.6% → 66.1%
claims.text: Replacing the action-selection step of a τ-bench tool agent with Jev cut median episode time from 267.1 s to 160.6 s but lowered success from 77.6% to 66.1% and raised the 95th-percentile time from 695.5 s to 816.0 s, as local decision errors accumulated over trajectories.
limitations: One run per task; two environments.

claims.headline: Near the number, rarely on it: 97% within ±1, 44% exact
claims.text: On tasks with a unique numerical answer, Jev landed within one of the exact value on 97% of repeating-division items but was exactly right on only 44% (39% on area inversion), while thinking LLMs recovered the exact values.
limitations: 100 items per task.

arxiv:2610.04345.title: System One Models for Wireless Decision-Making:Applications and Performance Evaluation
arxiv:2610.04345.relationship: Formalises System One models for bounded wireless control and benchmarks hosted Jev against generative LLMs and conventional baselines in wireless case studies.
arxiv:2610.04345.summary: Maps applicability across physical-layer control, radio resource management, mobility, network slicing and network operations, then measures decision quality and client-observed latency in receive-antenna selection and intent-conditioned RAN slicing, citing edge-service orchestration evidence from earlier work.
arxiv:2610.04345.task: Finite-action wireless control under latency constraints.
arxiv:2610.04345.finding: In receive-antenna selection Jev cut median response latency by up to 8.5 times against the evaluated LLMs but lost decision quality to stronger task-specific methods; in intent-conditioned RAN slicing it reached utility comparable to the LLMs with more than 3.5 times lower median latency. Faster decisions did not necessarily mean lower end-to-end service latency.
caveats: Client-observed latency of a hosted service.
Edge-orchestration evidence comes from an earlier study by other authors, not a new experiment.

claims.headline: Wireless control: 3.5–8.5× faster than LLMs; quality depends on the task
claims.text: Jev cut median response latency by up to 8.5 times against generative LLMs in receive-antenna selection at a loss in decision quality to stronger task-specific methods, and matched the LLMs’ utility in intent-conditioned RAN slicing with more than 3.5 times lower median latency.
limitations: Client-observed latency; simulated scenarios.

arxiv:2610.04985.title: Hidden Risks of Jev: An Empirical Study of Security, Privacy, and Dual Use
arxiv:2610.04985.relationship: Systematic security and privacy study of Jev as an application decision layer, using the official API and the trainable open NanoJev.
arxiv:2610.04985.summary: Adapts prompt injection and universal adversarial suffixes to the Choice, binary and Score interfaces, implants backdoors in NanoJev through 5% training-data poisoning under SFT and RLCD, adapts membership, private-attribute and internal-knowledge inference, and examines dual use: four detection tasks on eight benchmarks plus jailbreak planning and model extraction.
arxiv:2610.04985.task: Security, privacy and dual use of typed decision layers.
datasets: Ticket-routing style application tasks (support routing, subscription cancellation, issue severity)
arxiv:2610.04985.finding: Context-ignoring injection reached 96.5% attack success against Jev on support routing and Jev-specific injections reached 100% on subscription cancellation and at least 96.8% on issue severity; backdoors implanted by poisoning NanoJev succeeded on over 89% of targeted inputs while clean accuracy stayed at 90.5–94.0%; as a detector Jev reached ROC-AUC 0.95–1.0 on all eight benchmarks, and the same capability supported jailbreak planning and model extraction.
caveats: Backdoor and membership experiments use the open NanoJev, not the hosted model.
Application tasks constructed by the authors.

claims.headline: Typed outputs, hijacked inputs: up to 100% injection success
claims.text: Text injected into the application state redirected Jev’s typed decisions: context-ignoring injection reached 96.5% attack success on support routing, and two Jev-specific injections, which claim the state is outdated and add false information, reached 100% on subscription cancellation and at least 96.8% on issue severity.
limitations: Author-built application tasks.

claims.headline: Poisoned open checkpoints: >89% targeted redirection, clean accuracy intact
claims.text: Poisoning 5% of NanoJev’s training records with SFT or RLCD implanted backdoors that redirected over 89% of targeted inputs in most settings while clean accuracy stayed at 90.5–94.0%; RLCD generally gave higher attack success than SFT.
limitations: Open NanoJev; hosted model not poisoned.

claims.headline: As a guard: ROC-AUC 0.95–1.0 on eight detection benchmarks
claims.text: Used as a detector, Jev reached ROC-AUC 0.95–1.0 on all eight prompt-injection, jailbreak, harmful-content and AI-text benchmarks, with calibrated accuracy of 87–99% on the six security benchmarks, while open NanoJev was near chance on several.
limitations: Public benchmarks; thresholds calibrated per benchmark.

arxiv:2610.05107.title: SearchJev: A Fast and Calibrated System-1 Model for Search Agents
arxiv:2610.05107.relationship: Fast, calibrated System One model for the short decisions of search agents, trained with soft labels and paired with a System-2 planner.
arxiv:2610.05107.summary: Scores legal options for relevance, evidence sufficiency and search actions without generation, learns from uncertain supervision with Soft-Label Learning for Calibrated Decisions (SLCD), delegates low-confidence judgments to System 2, and introduces SearchDecision-Bench (six decision types); hosted Jev 1.13 is an external comparator.
arxiv:2610.05107.task: Search-agent decisions: relevance, sufficiency, routing, rewriting, verification.
arxiv:2610.05107.finding: SearchJev beat same-size Qwen3.5 autoregressive models in decision quality while deciding 5.2–5.3 times faster with 41–74% lower average ECE; on held-out data it exceeded hosted Jev on query rewriting (and the 4B model on relevance) while Jev stayed stronger on routing and verification; in BrowseComp-Plus the dual-system agents cut median active search time 3.7–4.7-fold and raised answer accuracy from 45% to up to 54%.
caveats: Authors’ own benchmark.
Jev compared through its API on the same items.

claims.headline: Task-specialised open model beats Jev on rewriting, trails on routing
claims.text: On held-out search-decision datasets, both SearchJev models exceeded hosted Jev 1.13 on query rewriting and the 4B model also led on relevance, while Jev remained stronger on routing and verification; against same-size Qwen3.5 autoregressive models SearchJev decided 5.2–5.3 times faster with 41–74% lower average ECE.
limitations: Authors’ benchmark and training data.

claims.headline: Search agent: 3.7–4.7× faster, accuracy 45% → 54%
claims.text: In BrowseComp-Plus, dual-system agents that let SearchJev take confident short decisions cut median active search time 3.7–4.7-fold and output tokens 3.3–4.8-fold against a System-2-only agent while raising answer accuracy from 45% to up to 54%; against a Jev 1.13 agent the 0.8B model used fewer calls and less time at the same accuracy.
limitations: One deep-research benchmark.

arxiv:2610.06354.title: GraphDecide: Benchmarking System One Models on Graph Tasks
arxiv:2610.06354.relationship: Model-independent benchmark of System One models on graph cognition, graph-text prediction and graph construction.
arxiv:2610.06354.summary: Combines structural task profiles, matched graph-only/text-only/joint inputs and heuristic-proposal controls over fourteen model–interface configurations (Jev, Kev, Laya and language-model adapters) on small undirected graphs, ogbn-arxiv, STaRK-Prime and construction tasks such as routing and MaxCut.
arxiv:2610.06354.task: Graph decisions: structure queries, node classification, retrieval and construction.
arxiv:2610.06354.finding: Jev answered every adjacency query correctly and did well on cycle, connectivity and distance, yet reached only 67.80% on exact degree and 61.25% on articulation points; joint graph-text input did not consistently improve prediction, and feasible constructions did not imply good solutions.
caveats: Small public instances; no claim for large or dynamic graphs.
Shares authors with PixelJev.

claims.headline: Reads every edge; counts degree right 68% of the time
claims.text: Jev answered every adjacency query correctly and performed relatively well on cycle, connectivity and distance judgments, but reached only 67.80% on exact degree and 61.25% on articulation points, so recognising an explicitly listed edge did not establish neighbour counting or connectivity reasoning.
limitations: Small graphs.

arxiv:2610.06625.title: JEV versus LLMs: Accuracy, Cost and Calibration on Seven Political Science Replications
arxiv:2610.06625.relationship: Compares hosted Jev with GPT-6 Luna, Qwen3.8-27B and published human and LLM coding on seven political-science text-analysis replications.
arxiv:2610.06625.summary: Replicates seven published annotation and scaling tasks, scoring Jev, a mid-tier commercial LLM and an open-weight model against human coding, and compares accuracy, billed cost and the calibration of Jev’s probabilities with LLM token probabilities.
arxiv:2610.06625.task: Annotation and scaling of political text.
baselines: Published human coders and LLM results
arxiv:2610.06625.finding: Jev matched or came close to both LLMs across tasks, but had no cost advantage over GPT-6 Luna at batch prices because it billed 1.2–3.3 times as many input tokens per decision; asked once, its probabilities were better calibrated than GPT-6 Luna’s token probabilities but not consistently better than Qwen3.8-27B’s.
caveats: Seven tasks from one discipline.
No code release located.

versions.note: Version string reported by the endpoint.

claims.headline: Same accuracy, no cost advantage at batch prices
claims.text: Across seven political-science replications, Jev matched or came close to GPT-6 Luna and Qwen3.8-27B against human coding, but had no cost advantage over GPT-6 Luna at OpenAI’s batch prices: it bills the question and every option as input, 1.2–3.3 times as many input tokens per decision as Luna, which wrote about four output tokens per answer.
limitations: Prices at the time of study.

claims.headline: Better calibrated than a commercial LLM, not than an open one
claims.text: When each question was asked once, Jev’s probabilities were better calibrated than GPT-6 Luna’s token probabilities but not consistently better than those of the open-weight Qwen3.8-27B.
limitations: Human coding as the benchmark.

arxiv:2610.06744.title: ufakzeka-karar: An Open Turkish Typed-Decision Model with Order-Invariant Option Scoring
arxiv:2610.06744.relationship: Open Turkish typed-decision model (182M parameters) with order-invariant option scoring and an expected-error “not sure” signal, running on one CPU thread.
arxiv:2610.06744.summary: Builds on the lab’s ufakzeka-1-base with a head that scores each option blind to the others at shared positions, trains with proper scoring rules on soft targets, compares a sequential head and REINFORCE, and reports results on HakemBench with disclosure of test-informed training.
arxiv:2610.06744.task: Turkish typed decisions with order invariance and abstention signals.
arxiv:2610.06744.finding: Scoring options blind to each other made answers independent of order by construction, while a sequential head trained on shuffled options changed 2.3–2.8% of answers when only the order changed; REINFORCE lost 0.102 macro-F1 to cross-entropy. The released model ranks 7th of 16 on HakemBench (composite 0.660) at a median of 102.5 ms on one CPU thread, and temperature scaling raised held-out calibration error (0.027 → 0.045).
caveats: Numbers are not blind: training data and the final run were shaped by reading test results.
Benchmark and model by the same author.
One human annotator.

claims.headline: Order invariance by construction; sequential heads still flip 2–3%
claims.text: A head that scores each option blind to the others made the 182M-parameter Turkish model order-invariant by construction, whereas a sequential head trained with shuffled options changed 2.3–2.8% of its answers when only the option order changed; the released model answers in a median 102.5 ms on one CPU thread.
limitations: Same author built the benchmark; results not blind.

arxiv:1901.04085.title: Passage Re-ranking with BERT
arxiv:1901.04085.role: Cross-encoder reranking with BERT: a query–passage pair in, one relevance probability out — the template for scoring a supplied candidate without generating text.

arxiv:2506.12181.title: Generative or Discriminative? Revisiting Text Classification in the Era of Transformers
arxiv:2506.12181.role: Controlled comparison of autoregressive, masked-LM, diffusion and encoder classifiers over fixed label sets, covering sample efficiency, calibration and ordinality — the trade-offs typed decision models inherit.

arxiv:2312.06674.title: Llama Guard: LLM-based Input-Output Safeguard for Human-AI Conversations
arxiv:2312.06674.role: Safety classification over a fixed taxonomy, read from the probability of a single safe/unsafe token: the guardrail pattern that typed yes/no questions are compared against.

arxiv:2501.18837.title: Constitutional Classifiers: Defending against Universal Jailbreaks across Thousands of Hours of Red Teaming
arxiv:2501.18837.role: Input and output classifiers trained from a written constitution to gate a frontier model against universal jailbreaks: the deployed policy-gate role that typed binary questions are proposed for.

arxiv:2203.02155.title: Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback
arxiv:2203.02155.role: Reward models that score a whole response with one scalar in a single pass, trained from human preferences: an early, widely deployed non-generative judgment head.

arxiv:2303.08774.title: GPT-4 Technical Report
arxiv:2303.08774.role: Reports that the pre-trained model was well calibrated and that post-training reduced calibration — the observation that calibration-oriented decision training responds to.

arxiv:2507.16806.title: Beyond Binary Rewards: Training LMs to Reason About Their Uncertainty
arxiv:2507.16806.role: Reinforcement learning with a calibration (Brier) reward alongside correctness, so a reasoning model’s stated confidence is trained to be calibrated: a published precedent for proper-scoring rewards in RL training of language models.

arxiv:2601.13284.title: Balancing Classification and Calibration Performance in Decision-Making LLMs via Calibration Aware Reinforcement Learning
arxiv:2601.13284.role: Shows that RL with verifiable rewards makes decision-making LLMs overconfident while supervised fine-tuning calibrates better, and proposes calibration-aware RL for decision tokens.

arxiv:2502.09992.title: Large Language Diffusion Models
arxiv:2502.09992.role: A masked diffusion language model that fills many positions in parallel: the reference point for diffusion readouts used by some open Jev-like projects.

arxiv:2506.17298.title: Mercury: Ultra-Fast Language Models Based on Diffusion
arxiv:2506.17298.role: Commercial diffusion language models that predict many tokens in parallel, reported as up to ten times faster than speed-optimised frontier models: a reference for non-autoregressive speed claims.

arxiv:2309.06180.title: Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention
arxiv:2309.06180.role: PagedAttention and KV-cache sharing for LLM serving: explains why several questions over one shared state can cost little more than one, independently of the readout.

arxiv:2310.03714.title: DSPy: Compiling Declarative Language Model Calls into Self-Improving Pipelines
arxiv:2310.03714.role: Declarative typed signatures compiled into prompts and self-improving pipelines: the programming-model alternative to a hosted typed-decision API.

arxiv:2408.02442.title: Let Me Speak Freely? A Study on the Impact of Format Restrictions on Performance of Large Language Models
arxiv:2408.02442.role: Finds that format restrictions can lower LLM reasoning accuracy: typed outputs should be compared with unconstrained answers, not only with constrained decoding.

arxiv:2010.06002.title: Thinking Fast and Slow in AI
arxiv:2010.06002.venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence 2021, 35(17), 15042-15046
arxiv:2010.06002.role: A research agenda built on the fast/slow (System 1 / System 2) distinction from cognitive science, which the “System One” product category borrows.

arxiv:2609.33992.title: GateDrain: Availability Attacks and Admission-Side Defense for Confidence-Gated Edge-Cloud Inference
arxiv:2609.33992.role: Shows that confidence-gated edge–cloud inference opens an availability attack: bounded perturbations lower confidence and push requests into a shared cloud queue, degrading tail latency for everyone; proposes admission-side budgets.

arxiv:2609.35039.title: Do Not Cut When Uncertain: Rejectable and Calibrated Decision Heads for VLA Policies in Robotic Harvesting
arxiv:2609.35039.role: Adds a typed, rejectable and calibrated decision head to a frozen vision-language-action policy for robotic harvesting, arguing that the right to refuse — not model scale — restores reliability under occlusion.

arxiv:2610.02516.title: Student-Guided Teacher Distillation for Efficient LLM Task Routing: Positioning Against Jev-Style System-1 Classifiers
arxiv:2610.02516.role: Distils a compact classifier that shortlists 60 task categories for a zero-shot NLI reranker, positioned as a documented alternative to System One classifiers whose training is undocumented.

arxiv:2610.01231.title: Judgement in the Age of Jev: From Evaluation Scarcity to Evaluation Abundance
arxiv:2610.01231.role: Perspective essay proposing a conditional Jevons hypothesis for machine evaluation: much cheaper evaluation may raise its organisational use where demand is latent, while shared criteria and errors can scale mistakes.

arxiv:2609.32160.title: Typed Decision Models: An Early Evidence Audit and Evaluation Checklist
arxiv:2609.32160.role: An early evidence audit of 28 studies posted 19–24 September 2026, concluding that the typed readout has not yet shown an accuracy advantage over comparable label-probability readouts, that the clearest gains are latency and cost, and proposing a 14-item evaluation checklist.

arxiv:2610.06425.title: SoK: Semantic Decision Engines in Network Control Loops
arxiv:2610.06425.role: Systematises 139 paper families on semantic decision engines in network control loops: of 50 that claim to fit a control loop or time budget, four support the claim with matched measurement, and bounded tests show queueing can turn every isolated deadline hit into a miss.

arxiv:2610.07953.title: Benchmarking System One Models in Online Moderation
arxiv:2610.07953.relationship: Evaluates hosted Jev and the open Laya as content-moderation decision models under controlled information conditions.
arxiv:2610.07953.summary: Separates written rules, retrieved precedents and restrictions on the candidate answer space across five moderation benchmarks, and tests whether Choice confidence supports selective review.
arxiv:2610.07953.task: Policy-violation detection with exact rule selection, and harmful-content detection.
arxiv:2610.07953.finding: With the full rule inventory held fixed, retrieved precedents raised Jev’s exact policy-selection accuracy by 12.35, 5.20 and 22.20 points on three evaluations while Laya gained little or lost; precedents raised Jev’s AUROC on OLID (.789 → .816), HateXplain (.749 → .755) and ModerationBench (.893 → .936 with Choice), and its confidence supported selective review (71.9% of ModerationBench decisions at confidence ≥ 0.8, with 94.3% accuracy), although it was not consistently calibrated.
caveats: Two SOM implementations only; generative LLMs appear as published reference points, not under the same conditions.
ModerationBench media are replaced by machine-generated captions.

data.note: Public benchmarks; captions generated by the authors.
data.label: Available

claims.headline: Precedents help Jev pick the right rule (+5 to +22 points); Laya barely moves
claims.text: With the complete rule inventory held fixed, adding five retrieved precedents raised Jev’s exact-match moderation accuracy by 12.35 points on six large PluRule communities, 5.20 points on the PluRule test intersection and 22.20 points on HateModerate, while Laya changed by −1.4 to +1.4 points on PluRule; with Noul questions, precedents raised Jev’s AUROC on OLID from .789 to .816 but lowered Laya’s from .800 to .702.
limitations: Matched contrasts on public benchmarks; generative LLMs not run under the same conditions.

claims.headline: Jev confidence supports selective review; Laya’s barely ranks errors
claims.text: Jev’s Choice confidence ranked its own errors with correctness AUC .628–.823 across five benchmarks; at confidence ≥ 0.8 it kept 45.0% of six-community PluRule decisions at 79.5% accuracy (65.1% overall) and 71.9% of ModerationBench decisions at 94.3% accuracy (86.7% overall), whereas Laya’s confidence ranked errors at AUC .560–.593 and covered 2.0–19.2% of decisions at that threshold.
limitations: The authors note that confidence is not consistently calibrated.

arxiv:2610.07716.title: Readout Stability in Prefill-Only Decision Models:Zero-Label Prediction and Inference-Time Compute Allocation
arxiv:2610.07716.relationship: Identifies a structural property of open prefill-only decision models and turns it into rules for spending inference-time compute.
arxiv:2610.07716.summary: Shows that after a menu-only change the accuracy of a prefill-only decision model can be predicted from the cached first-pass distribution (restrict, renormalise, take the argmax), tests the property on seven open decision-model families against generative controls, and compares extra passes, re-asking, cascades and menu curation at matched cost.
arxiv:2610.07716.task: Candidate-menu interventions and inference-time compute allocation.
baselines: Qwen3-4B-Instruct and Qwen3-8B (generative, next-token option scores)
arxiv:2610.07716.finding: Across seven open decision-model families, accuracy after a menu-only change was predicted from the first pass within 4.2 points (exactly for one family), while same-scale generative models erred by 1.6–15.8 points; extra order-permuted passes cut calibration error by 67% but added almost no accuracy, a confidence cascade to a larger sibling beat every re-ask scheme at matched cost, and a 0.8B model on a curated five-candidate menu reached 95.4% on CLINC150 against 80.0% for a 4B model on all 150 labels.
caveats: Open models only; hosted Jev was not tested.
Residuals are larger and one-sided on label spaces dense with near-duplicates.

data.note: Public datasets with the released code.
data.label: Available

claims.headline: Menu changes are predictable offline for decision models, not for generative LLMs
claims.text: Across 91 menu-only interventions on seven open decision-model families, restricting the cached first-pass distribution to the new menu predicted post-intervention accuracy within 4.2 points (exactly for the Open-Jev family), whereas the same estimator erred by 1.6–15.8 points on same-scale generative models and a probability-level variant erred by 21.0 points.
limitations: Open models only.

claims.headline: Extra passes buy calibration, not accuracy; escalate and curate instead
claims.text: Averaging sixteen order-permuted passes lowered expected calibration error by 67% but changed accuracy by at most 3.83 points (pooled +1.2); escalating the least-confident items from Kev-0.8B to larger siblings reached the 9B model’s single-pass accuracy at 1.0–6.3 forward units instead of 11, and on CLINC150 a 0.8B model on a curated five-candidate menu reached 95.4% against 80.0% for a 4B model on the full 150-label menu.
limitations: Compute measured in forward units of the smallest model.

arxiv:2610.07730.title: SanSi: A Looped Typed Decision Model for System 1.5 Thinking
arxiv:2610.07730.relationship: Builds a looped open typed decision model and measures what looping adds, with hosted Jev as an external reference.
arxiv:2610.07730.summary: Turns a language model pre-trained to loop (Ouro) into a typed decision model whose option probabilities are read and trained after every loop, compares it with non-looped models trained on the same data and recipe, tests reasoning depth on program-generated tasks and uses it as a reward model for reinforcement learning.
arxiv:2610.07730.task: Typed decisions across classification, multi-step reasoning, uncertain evidence, long documents and knowledge questions.
baselines: SmolLM2-1.7B and Ouro-1.4B single pass (same recipe)
arxiv:2610.07730.finding: Eight loops raised accuracy from 58.4% to 72.0% at fixed shape, data and recipe (+13.5 points), within 1.8 points of a single-pass model three times larger, and extended solvable reasoning depth beyond training; hosted Jev, not trained on these data, scored 78.9% overall but gave a hard answer to 62.8% of items whose deciding evidence had been removed and fell from 100% to chance on liar chains as the number of steps grew.
caveats: Hosted Jev is a reference, not a controlled comparison: it was not trained on the authors’ data.
The looping gain rests on a backbone pre-trained to loop.
English test suite assembled from public datasets.

weights.note: No release of the trained models was found.
weights.label: Not located

claims.headline: Looping a small decision model: +13.5 points at 7.7× compute
claims.text: On 10,027 test decisions from 59 sources, applying the same layers eight times raised accuracy from 58.4% (a non-looped model of the same shape, data and recipe) to 72.0% at 7.7 times the computation; calibration error was lowest after three loops and rose again as confidence kept increasing on wrong answers, while detection of missing evidence improved (AUROC 0.835 → 0.935) and hard answers on evidence-removed items fell from 27.1% to 17.5%.
limitations: Three training seeds; differences of one or two points on small groups need their intervals.

claims.headline: Hosted Jev answers 63% of evidence-removed items and loses track after three steps
claims.text: Queried as a reference, hosted Jev (jev-1.13.0) answered 78.9% of the 10,027 test decisions correctly but gave a hard answer to 62.8% of 382 items whose deciding evidence had been removed (evidence AUROC 0.743); on liar chains its accuracy fell from 100% at one step to 62.5% at three and stayed near chance from six steps on, while its confidence stayed above its accuracy.
limitations: Single runs of the hosted model; not trained on the authors’ data.

arxiv:2610.08089.title: When Plans Change Answers: Formalizing Cost-Accuracy Optimization for Semantic Queries
arxiv:2610.08089.relationship: Formal treatment of query optimisation when semantic predicates are decided by calibrated decision models such as Jev.
arxiv:2610.08089.summary: Defines oracle semantics, physical plans as logical plans plus decision policies, output-level quality targets and a hierarchy of plan equivalence; propagates calibrated decision errors through joins by lineage, prices output error per tuple and illustrates the definitions with synthetic simulations.
arxiv:2610.08089.task: Cost–accuracy optimisation of semantic queries with escalation.
arxiv:2610.08089.finding: Weighting each calibrated decision’s expected error by its contribution to the output predicts a plan’s output quality without labels; in simulation, plans for the same query differed by up to three orders of magnitude in cost, selection pushdown with bands calibrated on the plan’s own candidates met the output target on 62% of instances against 96% for pull-up, per-tuple prices met the target at about a fifth of the cost of the best operator-level band, and an overconfident model predicted output precision 0.981 where 0.872 was realised.
caveats: Theory and synthetic simulation only; no Jev or LLM calls.
Assumes independent decisions and a perfect judge.

code.note: The paper names a simulation script but gives no public link.
code.label: Not located

claims.headline: Calibrated confidence prices query plans; overconfidence hides output errors
claims.text: In synthetic simulations, plans for the same semantic join differed by up to three orders of magnitude in cost; bands calibrated on each plan’s own candidates made selection pushdown meet the output target on 62% of instances against 96% for pull-up, per-tuple prices met an output-level target at 7,164 cost units against 37,256 for the cheapest operator-level band, and an overconfident decision model predicted output precision 0.981 where 0.872 was realised.
limitations: Synthetic workload designed to make each effect visible.

arxiv:2610.07327.title: SharedKV-BT: Node-Local Typed Decisions for Behavior-Tree Agents
arxiv:2610.07327.relationship: Combines a Jev-style typed-decision interface over an open decoder with behaviour-tree control for robot and computer-use agents.
arxiv:2610.07327.summary: Each active behaviour-tree node exposes only its stage’s fields and candidates; an open decoder scores complete candidates in parallel from a shared KV cache; external postconditions, not the model, decide progression and completion.
arxiv:2610.07327.task: Typed action decisions for robot manipulation, navigation and computer-use agents.
arxiv:2610.07327.finding: Exposing only the current node’s candidates raised correct joint typed decisions from 90/120 to 113/120 and closed-loop four-object completion from 0/30 to 18/30; prefix reuse alone cut decision latency 1.29–2.09-fold, and stage gating with external postconditions prevented out-of-order actions and premature completion, but an explicit ABSTAIN option rejected 28/30 invalid menus while choosing correctly in only 17/30 valid ones.
caveats: Open Qwen2.5-3B (and Qwen3-4B) readout; hosted Jev was not used.
Simulated robots and a small number of computer-use runs.

claims.headline: Node-local candidates: 113/120 correct decisions against 90/120
claims.text: In Adaptive PickPlace, exposing only the active behaviour-tree node’s fields raised correct joint skill–object decisions from 90/120 (all fields exposed) to 113/120 and closed-loop four-object completion from 0/30 to 18/30, at 128 ms against 316 ms per decision; with model scores held fixed, removing stage gating or the external postcondition let the agent act out of order or stop early in 10 of 15 saved states.
limitations: Saved states repeat across seeds; counts are descriptive.

claims.headline: ABSTAIN catches invalid menus but costs valid answers; order flips 46 of 120 picks
claims.text: With an explicit ABSTAIN candidate, complete-candidate scoring rejected 28 of 30 menus that contained no valid action but chose the correct action in only 17 of 30 valid menus (45/60 overall against 51/60 for autoregressive generation), and changing only the candidate order changed the selected value in 46 of 120 node-local states.
limitations: 60 held-out cases; one open model.

arxiv:2610.07177.title: CLM-as-a-Judge: Evaluating an Open Contrastive Decision Model on Public Judge Benchmarks
arxiv:2610.07177.relationship: Preregistered evaluation of an open contrastive System One model (CLM-v0.1-8B) and Laya as judges.
arxiv:2610.07177.summary: Scores CLM zero-shot and with fine-tuned heads on five preference benchmarks and one hallucination benchmark against generative, reward-model and trivial baselines under a frozen preregistration, measuring calibration, error detection, order and length bias and a confidence-gated cascade to a strong judge.
arxiv:2610.07177.task: Judging: pairwise and best-of-four preference, hallucination detection.
arxiv:2610.07177.finding: Zero-shot CLM scored 0.351–0.593 (at chance on RM-Bench and JudgeBench, one constant label on HaluEval) while a same-size reward model reached 0.764–0.976; raw confidences were overconfident by up to +0.401 but one pooled temperature brought ECE to at most 0.062, and order flips were 0.0002 against 0.2188 for the generative judge, yet a confidence-gated cascade escalated 92.3–100% of items to the strong judge.
caveats: Same author as the Laya reproduction (2609.33843).
Laya’s 512-token window truncates most inputs on four benchmarks.

versions.note: Pinned by revision hash in the ancillary files.

data.label: Available

claims.headline: Open contrastive decision model judges near chance, but ignores answer order
claims.text: Zero-shot, the open contrastive decision model CLM-v0.1-8B scored 0.351–0.593 as a judge, statistically indistinguishable from chance on RM-Bench and JudgeBench and one constant label on HaluEval, while a same-size reward model reached 0.764–0.976 and a generative judge 0.611–0.778; its decisions flipped under answer-order swap at 0.0002 against 0.2188 for the generative judge.
limitations: One open checkpoint, zero-shot; fine-tuned heads moved accuracy by −0.028 to +0.060.

claims.headline: Calibrated after one temperature, yet the gate escalates 92–100%
claims.text: Raw CLM confidences were overconfident by +0.235 to +0.401; one pooled temperature fitted on held-out calibration items brought ECE to 0.032–0.062, but at a preregistered 0.97 retention bar the confidence-gated cascade escalated 92.3–100% of items to the strong judge, because calibrated confidence about a near-chance judge leaves almost nothing to keep.
limitations: The strong judge is a hosted service whose configuration can change.

arxiv:2610.07019.title: Calibrated Answers About Randomized Trials From a 4-Billion-Parameter Open Model: A Registered Test and a License-Clean Release
arxiv:2610.07019.relationship: Registered test and licence-clean release of a 4B open typed-decision model for questions about randomised trials.
arxiv:2610.07019.summary: Fine-tunes Qwen3-4B-Base with LoRA and the Laya decision head on licence-clean Evidence Inference articles, decides the release by four criteria registered on OSF before test predictions, runs reading checks (no article, title only, arms exchanged) and tests handing uncertain answers to a larger model.
arxiv:2610.07019.task: Evidence Inference 2.0: the direction of a trial’s effect on an outcome.
datasets: Evidence Inference 2.0 (1,218 test prompts in 333 articles)
arxiv:2610.07019.finding: All four criteria registered before test predictions passed: ECE 0.0168 (limit 0.05), log loss below Gemma 4 31B-it by 0.1829 and macro-F1 0.9248 against 0.8668; reading checks showed macro-F1 0.4384 without the article, a gain from the title alone, and only 66.5% of direction answers reversed when intervention and comparator were exchanged.
caveats: EI test labels are public, so no evaluation of EI can be blind (author).
One question type; a research model, not for clinical use.

arxiv:2610.06985.title: CrystalJev: thinking fast and slow with atomistic foundation models for materials discovery
arxiv:2610.06985.relationship: Applies the typed-decision contract of System One models to atomistic foundation models for materials discovery.
arxiv:2610.06985.summary: Small heads on one unrelaxed forward pass of a frozen interatomic potential answer typed questions with probabilities calibrated on a small random slice, conformal procedures give finite-sample guarantees, and a value-of-information rule decides when a relaxation or a DFT calculation is worth its cost.
arxiv:2610.06985.task: Materials-discovery decisions: crystal stability and electronic, mechanical and molecular properties.
datasets: Matbench Discovery (MP reference set and WBM candidates; 65 models)
Registered prospective test with new DFT calculations
baselines: Each potential’s relax-and-threshold practice, recalibrated on the same slice
arxiv:2610.06985.finding: For MACE-MP-0 and CHGNet, one calibrated unrelaxed pass decided stability better than recalibrated relax-and-threshold (log-loss 0.191 against 0.247 and 0.196 against 0.266) at about a thirtieth of the cost, and slightly worse for four newer potentials; in a registered prospective test, single-pass forecasts calibrated only on existing data over-stated the stable fraction of unseen candidates (5.8%) by 0.8–2.1 points, with AUROC 0.965–0.982.
caveats: Not a language model and no Jev calls: the typed-decision contract is applied to frozen interatomic potentials.
Code and data are to be released on publication.

arxiv:2610.08155.title: Token-Efficient Multi-Agent Collaboration via System One-Guided Computational Division of Labor
arxiv:2610.08155.relationship: Multi-agent framework that hands bounded coordination decisions to an open System One model.
arxiv:2610.08155.summary: Laya decides what to inspect, which task to run next and when to stop, a small reader localises evidence, and GPT-4o workers do the open-ended reasoning; compared with twelve training-free baselines and ablated against random and GPT-based coordination.
arxiv:2610.08155.task: Multi-agent coordination for reasoning, knowledge QA, code generation and web QA.
arxiv:2610.08155.finding: S1-MAS reached the highest mean accuracy on six benchmarks (macro-average 93.97%, 0.85 points above DyLAN) while cutting GPT-4o tokens by 78.3–94.0% and latency by 58.2–91.7% against five multi-agent baselines; in ablation, Laya’s coordination decisions beat random choices from the same legal menus by only 1.83 points but matched a GPT-4o-mini controller’s accuracy with 75.5% fewer GPT tokens.
caveats: Gains combine the framework’s task construction, budgets and early stopping with the System One decisions.
No code release located.

claims.headline: Laya coordinates agents with 78–94% fewer GPT tokens; random choices trail by 1.8 points
claims.text: Across six benchmarks S1-MAS reached the highest mean accuracy (macro-average 93.97%) while using 78.3–94.0% fewer GPT-4o tokens and 58.2–91.7% lower latency than five multi-agent baselines; in a GPT-4o-mini ablation, Laya’s coordination decisions scored 84.17% against 82.34% for random choices from the same legal menus and 83.14% for a GPT controller that used about four times as many tokens.
limitations: Three seeds; tokens and latency include every GPT call.

arxiv:2610.08775.title: Agent in a Bottle: Can LLM Agents Turn Their Capabilities Into Cheap, Scalable Artifacts?
arxiv:2610.08775.relationship: Benchmark of LLM agents that turn a whole workload into a cheaper reusable solution, with hosted Jev as a zero-shot comparator.
arxiv:2610.08775.summary: Agents receive an unlabelled workload and fixed time, compute and API budgets and must deliver a reusable solution (for example a trained small model or a program); results are compared with zero-shot LLM inference, small-model distillation and zero-shot hosted Jev on the classification tasks.
arxiv:2610.08775.task: Amortising narrow repetitive workloads: attribute extraction, query–product relevance and AI-text detection.
baselines: Hosted Jev (jev-1.13.0), ESCI and RAID only
arxiv:2610.08775.finding: Strong zero-shot models did not reliably bottle (48 of 60 runs fell below their model’s zero-shot interval), but bottling could be far cheaper; against zero-shot Jev on 1,000-item samples, an Opus 5 solution reached 94% of Jev’s ESCI macro-F1 (0.499 against 0.531) at about a quarter of Jev’s projected full-workload cost, and a Gemini 3.1 Pro solution 97% of Jev’s RAID AUROC (0.822 against 0.846) at about 2% of its cost.
caveats: Jev’s cost is projected from a 1,000-item sample to the full workload.
Jev cannot answer the generative MAVE task.
